artigo.texto: Leading battery scientist promotes alternatives to expensive and scarce lithium amid EV sales surge A leading Chinese battery scientist has urged greater research into lithium alternatives for batteries, particularly sodium, to lower China’s dependence on rare, imported and costly metals. Though Chen Liquan, was speaking in regards to China, his sentiment should reverberate in Australia and the world as the Iran war exposes our reliance on imported essentials. Professor Chen received the Highest Science and Technology Award, sometimes called “China’s Nobel Prize”, from president Xi Jinping on 8 July. Chen specifically addressed the automotive industry at the ceremony, highlighting the need to insulate themselves from overseas supply shocks. Three quarters of China’s lithium is imported, a significant vulnerability for its car industry as it flourishes at home and abroad. Despite this, alternatives to lithium-ion batteries have been slow in coming. Sodium-ion batteries have surged ahead of solid-state batteries which, alongside flying cars, have been ‘around the corner’ for years. “Solid-state” refers to replacing the batteries’ liquid electrolyte with a solid like ceramic, enabling smaller and less flammable batteries. Though Toyota and Nissan believe theirs will be ready by 2028, International Energy Agency analyst Teo Lombardo, speaking to Yale Environment 360, believes 2030 is more realistic, and that solid-state batteries will remain expensive and relatively niche. Battery juggernaut CATL, supplier of approximately a third of the world’s EV batteries, appears to have heeded the professor’s call, announcing in late June that its sodium-ion batteries were nearing price parity with its lithium-ion mainstays. Though Changan – owners of Deepal who, in joint venture with Mazda, develops the latter’s 6e sedan and CX-6e medium SUV – hopes to bring sodium-battery-powered cars to market this year, their first consumer application could well be trucks. Car News China reports the new batteries retain at least 90 percent of their range at -20°C; this is 80 percent at best for lithium batteries, a boon for truckies in China’s bitingly cold north. Sodium atoms are twice as big and three times heavier than lithium atoms, requiring sodium-ion batteries to be bigger and heavier than lithium-ion ones to deliver the same range. But as sodium is much cheaper and easier to source than lithium, applications where size and weight are less of a concern, such as stationary storage, are very promising. Changan is betting some customers will accept sodium batteries’ extra weight in exchange for cold-weather performance and, in time, lower prices. artigo.texto: Chinese energy storage provider Jinko ESS has agreed to supply 34 battery storage systems with a combined capacity of 18 megawatt-hours (MWh) for a telecommunications project in Mali, adding to investment aimed at reducing diesel dependence across Africa’s mobile networks. Announced on 17 October 2026, the agreement covers Jinko ESS’s SunGiga G2 Plus systems. The company, a subsidiary of solar manufacturer Jinko Solar, has not disclosed the project partner, contract value or installation sites. The announcement comes as telecommunications operators and infrastructure providers seek more reliable and cost-effective ways to power network equipment in markets where grid electricity can be inconsistent and fuel delivery expensive. The deal reflects a wider shift in how energy is managed across Africa’s telecommunications sector. Mobile towers require continuous power to maintain voice and data services, including in rural and remote areas where grid connections may be weak or unavailable. Diesel generators have traditionally filled that gap, but their operating costs, maintenance requirements and exposure to fuel supply disruptions have encouraged companies to consider solar generation and battery storage. According to a July 2025 analysis by CrossBoundary Energy, approximately 70% of Africa’s 500,000 telecommunications towers rely on diesel. At remote sites, fuel can account for between 30% and 60% of operating expenditure. The cost of transporting fuel adds further pressure, particularly where sites are difficult to reach or supply routes are disrupted. These expenses can make energy one of the most significant controllable costs in operating a telecommunications network. Battery storage can help address some of these challenges by storing electricity generated from solar panels or drawn from the grid when available, then supplying power when generation falls or the grid fails. In hybrid systems, batteries can reduce the hours diesel generators need to operate, while solar generation can lower the amount of fuel consumed. The extent of the savings depends on local solar resources, electricity demand, battery configuration, generator efficiency and the reliability of existing power infrastructure. Jinko ESS has not disclosed whether the 34 SunGiga G2 Plus systems will be installed alongside new solar capacity, integrated into existing hybrid power systems or deployed as part of a broader network upgrade. Without details on the sites and system configuration, the project’s expected reduction in diesel consumption, operating costs and emissions cannot yet be quantified. The agreement comes amid a series of investments in renewable energy for Mali’s telecommunications infrastructure. In March 2025, the Facility for Energy Inclusion (FEI) and Norfund signed financing agreements totalling US$40 million with Communication and Renewable Energy Infrastructure (CREI), an asset management company specialising in energy infrastructure for telecommunications. The financing supports CREI’s Telecom Energy Service Company model, under which it develops, builds, operates and maintains energy assets for mobile network operators. CREI said the wider investment programme would modernise telecommunications tower infrastructure in Mali through hybrid renewable energy systems incorporating solar and battery storage. The approach allows network operators to obtain energy services without necessarily financing and managing all the underlying power equipment themselves. For providers of distributed energy infrastructure, such arrangements can create opportunities to aggregate sites and deliver energy solutions at scale. Further financing followed in November 2025, when the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and the West African Development Bank (BOAD) announced an €80 million financing package for Orange Mali. The investment is intended to support the installation of 300 new 4G towers, expand fibre connectivity and improve access to digital services, particularly in rural areas. As part of the project, Orange Mali is expected to replace diesel generators with solar-powered systems, with the IFC estimating that the change will reduce carbon dioxide emissions by more than 8,000 tonnes annually. These investments demonstrate how energy infrastructure and digital connectivity are increasingly linked. Reliable mobile networks support financial services, education, business transactions and access to information. Where electricity supply is unstable, network operators must invest in backup power and fuel logistics to maintain service. Those costs can affect the commercial viability of expanding coverage into remote communities, where average revenues per user may be lower and infrastructure more expensive to operate. The transition to solar and battery-based systems is therefore not only an emissions issue. It is also a question of network resilience and the economics of extending digital services. Lower fuel consumption can reduce exposure to price volatility and delivery delays, while battery systems can provide a buffer against grid interruptions. However, energy storage introduces its own costs, including equipment procurement, replacement over time, maintenance and the need for appropriate system monitoring. For investors and equipment suppliers, the opportunity lies in delivering solutions that remain reliable under local operating conditions. Telecom sites can differ considerably in electricity demand, climate, security risks and accessibility. Systems installed in remote locations must be designed for limited maintenance access and must maintain performance over years of continuous operation. Procurement price alone will not determine the long-term economics; equipment durability, warranties, service capacity and battery lifecycle costs will also matter. artigo.texto: Nordeste avança como polo de data centers e deve atrair quase 30% dos novos investimentos do setor há 3 dias 5 min de leitura O Nordeste avança na instalação de centros de processamento de dados, conhecidos como data centers, impulsionado pela crescente demanda por capacidade computacional e pela disponibilidade de energia renovável. O movimento amplia a presença do setor para além do eixo Rio-São Paulo e coloca a região em posição estratégica para receber novos investimentos em infraestrutura digital. Uma projeção da Tendências Consultoria, divulgada em junho, indica que o Produto Interno Bruto (PIB) nordestino deve crescer, em média, 3,3% ao ano entre 2028 e 2035. O resultado ficaria acima dos 2,4% estimados para a economia brasileira no mesmo período. A expansão econômica ocorre em paralelo ao crescimento do mercado de data centers no país. A expectativa é que a capacidade brasileira dobre até 2030, enquanto parte significativa dos empreendimentos em construção já tem sua capacidade contratada antecipadamente. Dos 660 megawatts (MW) em capacidade de data centers que estavam em construção no Brasil, 56% já haviam sido pré-locados, ou seja, reservados por clientes antes da conclusão das obras. Outro fator que pode estimular a expansão é o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (Redata), programa de incentivos sancionado pelo presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) em setembro. A medida busca estimular a instalação e a ampliação desses empreendimentos no território nacional. Nordeste ganha espaço nos investimentos em infraestrutura O desempenho econômico regional também reforça as perspectivas para o setor. Entre agosto de 2025 e julho de 2026, a atividade econômica do Nordeste cresceu 2,5%, segundo análise do Escritório Técnico de Estudos Econômicos do Nordeste (Etene), vinculado ao Banco do Nordeste (BNB). O resultado superou a média nacional, de 1,5%, e colocou a região entre as que apresentaram maior crescimento no período, ao lado do Sul. No setor energético, as perspectivas também apontam para uma participação crescente do Nordeste. Projeções da Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE), incluídas no Plano Decenal de Expansão de Energia 2036, indicam que a região poderá atrair quase 30% dos novos investimentos em data centers de grande porte. A disponibilidade de energia proveniente de fontes renováveis, principalmente eólica e solar, é um dos fatores que favorecem essa expansão. O avanço acompanha mudanças no consumo de eletricidade, o crescimento econômico e a necessidade cada vez maior de processamento de dados para serviços digitais e aplicações de inteligência artificial. Fortaleza abriga o maior data center em operação no Nordeste Na capital do Ceará, um dos principais exemplos dessa expansão é o TFOR3, conhecido como “Mega Lobster”. O empreendimento pertence à Tecto Data Centers, plataforma controlada pelo BTG Pactual e ligada à V.tal, e foi inaugurado em outubro de 2025, na região da Praia do Futuro. O centro de dados tem capacidade final projetada de 20 MW, com ampliação prevista em etapas, de acordo com a demanda dos clientes. A empresa pretende elevar a capacidade inicial de 4 MW para 8 MW até o começo de 2027. A estrutura foi desenvolvida para atender aplicações que exigem grande capacidade de processamento e transmissão de informações, como inteligência artificial, serviços de computação em nuvem e distribuição de conteúdo digital. O empreendimento possui três andares, sistema próprio de resfriamento, geradores de energia e baterias. Esses recursos ajudam a manter os equipamentos funcionando caso ocorram falhas na distribuição de eletricidade. O local conta com dez data halls, áreas destinadas à instalação dos servidores utilizados pelos clientes. Esses ambientes concentram os equipamentos responsáveis por armazenar, processar e transmitir grandes volumes de dados. Além da unidade TFOR3, a Tecto mantém outros dois data centers em Fortaleza, um no Rio de Janeiro e três em Barranquilla, na Colômbia. Para acelerar sua expansão na América Latina, a companhia prevê investimentos estimados em US$ 2 bilhões entre 2026 e 2028. Ceará também receberá projeto ligado ao TikTok Outro empreendimento de grande porte está em desenvolvimento no Complexo Industrial e Portuário do Pecém, também no Ceará. A empresa Omnia trabalha na implantação de um data center destinado a atender à ByteDance, companhia chinesa proprietária do TikTok. A primeira fase do projeto prevê capacidade de 200 MW, com início de operação planejado para 2027. O empreendimento reforça a posição do Ceará na disputa por investimentos em infraestrutura digital, setor que depende de grandes instalações, fornecimento confiável de eletricidade e conexões de telecomunicações capazes de atender à demanda de empresas e plataformas digitais. Data centers podem ajudar a aproveitar a energia excedente O crescimento do setor também desperta o interesse das empresas de geração de energia. A demanda adicional dos centros de processamento de dados pode contribuir para aproveitar parte da eletricidade disponível no sistema brasileiro que, em determinadas situações, não consegue ser totalmente utilizada. Gilberto Feldman, CEO da Engeform, afirmou que a chegada de novos data centers pode ajudar a reduzir os cortes de geração impostos pelo Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS), que atingem principalmente usinas eólicas e solares em determinadas circunstâncias. “Hoje nós temos uma sobra de energia no país, que inclusive contribui muito para os cortes, e a vinda dos data centers deve contribuir para a redução dos cortes”, afirmou o executivo. Segundo Feldman, a disponibilidade de recursos naturais permite ao Brasil oferecer eletricidade de fontes limpas e renováveis a preços competitivos. Para ele, o Nordeste apresenta condições favoráveis para atrair atividades de processamento de dados que necessitam de grandes volumes de energia. artigo.texto: VSL PowerHive to Launch 7.5 GWh Battery Storage Facility 19 Oct 2026 2 Min Read CW Team Share VSL PowerHive, a wholly owned subsidiary of Vikram Solar, plans to establish a 7.5 GWh per annum Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) assembly facility at Oragadam near Chennai in Tamil Nadu. The plant is scheduled for inauguration in January 2027, with commercial operations expected to begin in April 2027. It will initially cover approximately 165,000 square feet and can be expanded to 15 GWh in subsequent phases. The facility forms part of Vikram Solar’s plan to develop 30 GWh of total battery manufacturing capacity by 2030. The company is also planning a 7.5 GWh battery cell manufacturing programme from 2028, with the aim of creating an integrated domestic ecosystem covering cells and complete energy storage systems. The Oragadam plant will manufacture lithium iron phosphate-based BESS products for utility-scale and commercial and industrial applications. Its planned portfolio includes 5.016 MWh and 6.25 MWh liquid-cooled BESS containers, PowerHive P261 battery cabinets, utility-scale storage systems and renewable energy-integrated storage solutions. The operations will be developed under the Make in India initiative. The expansion comes as India increases its solar and wind power capacity and requires storage to manage renewable power variability, support grid stability and shift surplus electricity to periods of peak demand. Projections from the Central Electricity Authority indicate that the country will require approximately 47 GW of energy storage power capacity and 236 GWh of storage capacity by 2031–32, creating opportunities for domestic manufacturers and reducing dependence on imported technologies. VSL PowerHive is developing indigenous battery technologies and has initiated several patent filings to strengthen its intellectual property portfolio. Vikram Solar chairman and managing director Gyanesh Chaudhary said the facility would extend the company’s clean energy activities beyond solar generation technologies, while chief executive Arun Mittal said the phased expansion would build advanced domestic manufacturing capabilities. The project is also expected to create skilled employment, develop local expertise and support Tamil Nadu’s clean technology manufacturing ecosystem. artigo.texto: Data center opponents are holding a series of eight marches across Virginia to call for a statewide moratorium on their construction. On Monday, they’ll be marching in Danville, which is an interesting choice, since the region is slated to get at least 2,050 jobs over the coming years at a data center complex to be built at the Southern Virginia Megasite. If that number comes to fruition — and that is the number of permanent jobs, not construction jobs, that the performance agreement calls for — it would be the largest jobs announcement in Southside in, well, a long time. The Virginia Economic Development Partnership database goes back to 1990 and the largest is the 2,015 jobs slated for the Microporous battery plant that’s now under construction. It’s unusual to see people marching against jobs in a part of the state that has undergone decades of economic trauma with the loss of key industries. On the other hand, those data center jobs aren’t there yet, but the energy demands from data centers are — something that those in neighboring Pittsylvania County know well since that county has approved more solar projects than any other in the state, according to the Weldon Cooper Center for Public Service at the University of Virginia, and officials there have spoken openly about “solar fatigue.” To that extent, Southside is a good place to examine the tensions and trade-offs with data centers: jobs and tax revenue versus energy requirements. There’s also something of a class conflict at work: Virginia’s most affluent counties in Northern Virginia are now tiring of data centers but some of its poorest counties in rural Virginia see data centers as an opportunity for long-sought revenue. Two counties to the east of Danville is Mecklenburg, which has been able to use revenue from a Microsoft data center complex to build three new schools, something most rural counties can’t afford. Many rural counties see a potential moratorium as a case of the rich telling the poor they can’t have the same opportunities; on the other hand, individual counties aren’t responsible for meeting the state’s energy requirements. State Sen. Russet Perry, D-Loudoun County, whose district includes “Data Center Alley,” last week announced she’ll be introducing a bill to impose a three-year moratorium on data center development. That seems unlikely to become law. In an appearance at the Governor’s Summit on Rural Prosperity in Lexington, Gov. Abigail Spanberger said she’s against a statewide moratorium because some localities want data centers — and those who don’t can impose their own moratoriums at any time. I asked Perry about the implications of her proposed moratorium on the Stack project in Pittsylvania and here’s what she emailed me: “A recent Brookings study found that while data centers do create some jobs, the long-term employment gains are much more modest than industry claims suggest. Beside the questionable jobs numbers being put forward by the wealthiest corporations to ever exist, simultaneously we have depleting water tables and an unstable power grid in Virginia, largely caused by the strains of the data center industry. The people of Southside Virginia, like those across the commonwealth, deserve the security of knowing they will have clean water to drink and can turn on the lights in their homes. Those are resources every family across Virginia depends on.” Meanwhile, from Kevin Hughes of Stack Infrastructure, the developer of that 2,500-job Pittsylvania County project: “A data center moratorium doesn’t eliminate demand for digital infrastructure. It shifts where that infrastructure gets built and where the investment goes. Americans will continue creating data, businesses will continue adopting AI and demand for digital services will only grow. The question is whether we build the infrastructure to support that growth in a given locality, state or even in the United States, or increasingly rely on capacity elsewhere. This is about more than jobs and economic development. It’s about American competitiveness, the resilience of our digital infrastructure, and maintaining greater control over sensitive information. Communities should absolutely have a voice in how infrastructure is developed, and legitimate concerns deserve thoughtful, fact-based solutions. But restricting data center development won’t stop demand. It risks sending investment, innovation and opportunity somewhere else.” Those are the politics of a potential moratorium. What about the technicalities? That’s what I set out to explore today. What would happen if Virginia did impose a statewide moratorium? Or if enough localities imposed their own that much of the state was off-limits to data centers? The answer seems obvious and Hughes’ answer foreshadows it: Data centers would simply go somewhere else. Even without a moratorium, Virginia is on the verge of losing its crown as the world’s data center capital. The commercial real estate firm JLL recently reported that Texas now has almost as much data center capacity as Virginia — and is in the process of building more than we are. We can’t say that Virginia is losing data centers to Texas, but Texas is certainly gaining them at a faster rate now. That might simply be inevitable: Texas is a lot bigger geographically than Virginia so, as the saying goes, everything is bigger in Texas. Some might like a statewide moratorium, some might not. You might see the results of either policy in your power bill or your tax bill, but your experience as a data consumer would not change. You could still swipe your card at the gas pump, you could still upload your funny cat video to TikTok, you could still watch all the Netflix movies you want and never notice which data centers all that data is being routed through. TikTok uses a lot of servers in Virginia now, but until 2023 it stored some of its American data in Singapore. Some of your other online transactions might already be happening on servers overseas

artigo.texto: Neocloud operator Nscale’s IPO plans could be at risk after Microsoft cancels UK data center project British neocloud startup Nscale Global Holdings Ltd.’s plans to launch an initial public offering in the U.S. have suffered a massive setback after its biggest customer Microsoft Corp. pulled out of a critical data center deal this weekend. A report in The Telegraph today said Microsoft has terminated an agreement to rent artificial intelligence infrastructure at the company’s planned facility in Loughton, Essex. The project, which had already been beset by repeated construction delays, has effectively been derailed after U.K. grid officials told Nscale they would not be able to provide adequate power to the site until the 2030s. The cancellation of the deal comes at a time when Nscale is also experiencing construction problems at another facility in Norway. That site has reportedly struggled with cooling system leaks, regulatory hurdles and a fire. A spokesperson for Nscale told The Telegraph that the company’s relationship with Microsoft remains “strong and long-term,” and insisted that the grid issue has no impact on several other contracts it has signed with the Windows software giant. “We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the U.K., and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the U.K.,” the spokesperson said. Nscale announced the facility in September 2025 alongside three other projects as part of a reported $24 billion contract it had signed with Microsoft. The other projects included sites in Texas, Portugal and a second facility in Norway, located close to an existing data center the company already operates. Those projects are all still believed to be on track. However, the future of the Loughton facility is now up in the air. Nscale originally announced plans to install 23,040 Nvidia graphics processing units at the site by the first quarter of 2027, which would have provided an initial 50 megawatts of AI capacity. It also had plans to expand that to 90 megawatts if needed. $MSFT Microsoft has canceled an AI data center deal with Nvidia-backed Nscale in the UK 🤖❌ The facility was expected to house around 23,000 Nvidia GPUs, but electricity may not be available until the 2030s. Other deals between Microsoft and Nscale are not affected. pic.twitter.com/Fmeo7z04Ay — The Future Investors (@ftr_investors) October 18, 2026 The setback comes at a difficult time for Nscale, just a month after the company confidentially filed for an IPO with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. It has applied to list on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker symbol NSCL, and is reportedly hoping to raise $3 billion at a valuation of about $35 billion, well in excess of its private valuation of $15 billion. But with the loss of the Loughton facility, investors are going to be much more skeptical about betting on Nscale. One reason for investors to be nervous is that Microsoft is one of only two major customers Nscale currently has. Microsoft and Anthropic PBC account for approximately 85% of Nscale’s entire contract value, according to its IPO filing. Nscale is one of a number of so-called neoclouds, which are specialized cloud infrastructure providers that rival hyperscalers such as Amazon Web Services Inc., Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud. Other well known neoclouds include CoreWeave Inc. in the U.S. and Nebius Group N.V., which has a very strong presence in Europe. They have become popular bets with investors looking to capitalize on the AI boom, but their expansion plans are heavily dependent on being able to secure billions of dollars in funding to construct the data centers and procure the equipment that goes inside them. That leaves them extremely vulnerable should delivery schedules slip or projects end up being canceled. Despite the best efforts of Nvidia Corp., which has tried to create new avenues for Wall Street to fund the AI infrastructure buildout, there have been signs that securing financing has become more difficult. CoreWeave’s stock fell more than 25% last week on concerns about its financing needs. At the weekend, a Financial Times report warned of the growing nervousness investors have over America’s immense AI infrastructure build out, which many believe is propping up the broader U.S. economy. Cracks are appearing in America’s debt-laden $10tn AI infrastructure boom as project delays, public backlash and shaky investor confidence bring a reckoning for the data centre build-out underpinning the US economy https://t.co/UkrO7uUUuO pic.twitter.com/b8kRAMKvXL — Financial Times (@FT) October 18, 2026 Last week, the Australian firm Firmus Technologies Pty. Ltd. abandoned its own IPO plans after failing to attract sufficient demand from prospective investors. In recent weeks, there have been reports that even Oracle Corp. has struggled to finance some of its data center projects. The database giant last month sent a notice of “force majeure” to the developer of its planned facility in New Mexico, following reports that it was also struggling to secure a power source. Against this backdrop, Nscale’s planned IPO is sure to become a real test of investor’s appetite for yet more risky bets whose growth depends on infrastructure that’s still under construction. artigo.texto: France-based energy company ENGIE has reached financial close on the 150 MW/300 MWh Hazelwood Battery Energy Storage System expansion (HBESS 2) in Victoria, Australia. The project will increase the site's total battery capacity to 300 MW/450 MWh, including the existing 150 MW/150 MWh system operating since 2023. Located at the former Hazelwood Power Station, the expansion will use existing infrastructure to store electricity, including daytime solar generation, for dispatch during higher-demand periods. Sungrow will supply battery technology, while Elecnor will undertake balance-of-plant and associated infrastructure works. The project follows the site's coal power station closure in 2017 and comes ahead of the planned Yallourn Power Station closure. Construction is scheduled to begin in late 2026, with commercial operations targeted for 2028. artigo.texto: The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) drives new technological opportunities, but also increases pressure on natural resources. Data centers that enable model training and query processing require large amounts of electricity, water, and specialized equipment, whose impacts depend on the conditions of each facility. Although computer systems improve their energy efficiency, the increase in users and high-consumption applications can counteract these advances. According to estimates by Our World in Data, AI-dedicated data centers consumed around 0.5% of the world’s electricity in 2025 and could reach 1.5% by 2030. However, calculating the real impact remains complex. The location of facilities, the energy sources used, cooling technologies, and the lack of detailed public information make it difficult to establish a complete assessment of the environmental consequences of this industry. The risks of AI use for the environment One of the main challenges is electricity consumption. Although a text query may require relatively little energy, more demanding tasks, such as generating videos, demand much more computing resources. If the electricity comes from coal or natural gas, its use generates emissions that contribute to global warming. Additionally, some data centers resort to gas turbines and their own generators to ensure supply. These equipment can emit atmospheric pollutants, such as nitrogen oxides and fine particles, which deteriorate air quality and pose health risks to nearby communities. Water is another major concern, as it is used to cool equipment and also during electricity generation. An analysis published in March by scientists from the University of California in Riverside and other institutions estimated that U.S. data centers could consume up to 416 billion liters annually by 2030. The impact may be greater in regions already suffering from water scarcity. Noise, heat, and mineral extraction Local effects also include noise pollution caused by fans, cooling systems, and generators. In certain communities, persistent noise has led to complaints about its effects on quality of life. Furthermore, the heat released by these facilities could intensify urban heat islands. Research conducted in Phoenix, Arizona, detected temperature increases of up to 2.2 °C in neighborhoods downwind of some data centers, although more studies are needed to determine the extent of this phenomenon. On the other hand, IT infrastructure depends on minerals and metals used in semiconductors, servers, and storage systems. Their extraction can cause deforestation, water pollution, and emissions, while equipment replacement increases electronic waste, of which only about one-fifth is recycled globally. How to reduce the ecological footprint of artificial intelligence Experts point out that these impacts can be reduced through planning, regulation, and design decisions. Priority measures include supplying data centers with renewable energies, improving cooling efficiency, and avoiding installations in water-stressed areas. It is also essential to demand transparency about energy consumption, emissions, water use, and the origin of materials. In turn, extending the lifespan of equipment and recovering its components can reduce pressure on ecosystems. Finally, before authorizing new projects, it is necessary to evaluate their economic and social benefits against the local environmental costs. The challenge is to harness the capabilities of AI without transferring its impacts to communities or compromising the resources that future generations will need.

artigo.texto: The next decade of battery materials growth is likely to be shaped as much by regulation as by vehicle demand. According to IndexBox, the market for life cycle safe battery production chemicals is expected to keep expanding through 2035, supported by tougher compliance expectations in Europe and by automakers pressing suppliers to clean up their sourcing.The forecast points to a structural shift in how battery inputs are bought, processed and documented. Rather than treating chemicals as a narrow procurement item, cell makers and their upstream suppliers are increasingly being asked to prove that the materials used in production can stand up to scrutiny across the full value chain. That includes traceability, environmental controls and adherence to rules that are becoming more demanding as battery manufacturing scales up.Regulation is now a commercial driverThe most immediate catalyst is the European Union's battery regulatory framework, which has pushed sustainability and disclosure from the margins into the centre of industrial planning. For chemical suppliers, the compliance burden is no longer limited to product quality and pricing. Buyers are now looking for evidence that inputs align with life cycle safety requirements, a trend that is likely to influence sourcing decisions well beyond Europe.IndexBox said the market outlook is being reinforced by automaker supply chain mandates, which are adding another layer of pressure on suppliers. As carmakers seek to de-risk their battery ecosystems, chemical vendors are being pushed to meet tighter standards on safety, documentation and consistency. In practice, that can favour larger suppliers with better process control, audit readiness and the ability to serve multiple geographies from a single compliance framework.Gigafactory expansion is widening the addressable marketAt the same time, the build-out of gigafactories is expanding the volume of chemicals needed for battery production. Every new cell plant adds demand not only for core active materials but also for a range of supporting chemicals used in manufacturing, treatment and quality assurance. As capacity rises, so does the need for suppliers that can deliver at industrial scale without compromising on regulatory standards.This creates a dual effect. On one hand, scale-up increases volumes and opens the door to larger contracts. On the other, it raises the bar for operational discipline, because any compliance lapse can ripple quickly through high-volume battery supply chains. That dynamic is likely to reward producers that can combine capacity, consistency and documentation in a sector where procurement decisions increasingly carry reputational as well as technical risk.What the forecast means for chemical makersFor chemical companies serving the battery industry, the opportunity is not simply about selling more product. The market is moving toward a model in which compliance credentials, product stewardship and supply chain transparency are part of the offer itself. Suppliers that can demonstrate life cycle safety may find themselves better positioned as preferred vendors to battery makers and automakers alike.The wider implication is that battery chemicals are becoming a strategic layer in the energy transition, not just a supporting input. As governments tighten standards and manufacturers expand capacity, the market is likely to favour players that can adapt quickly to documentation-heavy procurement and cross-border regulatory demands.IndexBox's outlook suggests that this is still an early stage of a longer cycle. Through 2035, the combination of battery regulation, automotive sourcing rules and gigafactory investment is expected to keep the market on an upward path, with compliance increasingly tied to commercial competitiveness. For suppliers, the message is clear: growth will depend not only on chemistry, but also on the ability to prove that every step of production is safe, traceable and fit for the next generation of battery manufacturing. - Policy & Regulation - 3 min Read Battery chemical suppliers eye compliance-led growth through 2035 IndexBox expects the market for life cycle safe battery production chemicals to grow through 2035 as EU battery rules and automaker sourcing mandates reshape procurement. Gigafactory expansion is adding demand, but suppliers will need stronger compliance, traceability and documentation to win contracts. - Published On Oct 19, 2026 at 12:46 PM IST

artigo.texto: Pitt County planning staff is scheduled to present an assessment of the county’s existing data center ordinance as the commissioners weigh implementing a moratorium on the facilities. The presentation will take place during the Pitt County Board of Commissioners’ 6 p.m. meeting today at the county office building, 1717 W. Fifth St. Residents have lobbied the commissioners to establish a moratorium in an effort to prevent data centers from locating facilities in the unincorporated areas of the county. In order to adopt a moratorium, the board needs to identify a deficiency in its current regulations that it wants to fix, officials have said during previous discussions. Along with the presentation, planning staff wants input from the commissioners on their concerns, potential impacts or regulatory issues that weren’t addressed in the evaluation. If the board proceeds with the moratorium, it will have to hold a public hearing. Staff is proposing the hearing be held at the board’s Nov. 16 meeting. Zoning amendment The board also is set to hold a public hearing on a request to amend the county’s zoning ordinance so the use “Outdoor Farm and Construction Equipment Auction” can be added as a permitted use. The county planning board in September said it was consistent with the county’s Comprehensive Land Use Plan but recommended it only be allowed as a conditional use in the rural agricultural zoning district. This would require the planning board and board of commissioners to hold public hearings on the request before making a decision. Planning staff recommends it be a permit by right in the rural agricultural zoning district, which only requires staff approval. Other actions State Reps. Gloristine Brown and Tim Reeder will present the commissioners with a $250,000 grant. The commissioners’ agenda did not indicate what grant program made the award or how the money will be used. The board is scheduled to adopt a proclamation recognizing October as Domestic Violence Awareness Month. A representative of Inspire Placemaking Collective, a consultant working with the county to develop a unified development ordinance, is scheduled to provide an overview of the project, which is expected to take 14-18 months to complete.

artigo.texto: Those pushing for a statewide moratorium on data center development worked to amplify their case during a rally on the steps of the courthouse in Leesburg. Organized by the Piedmont Environmental Council, the hour-long event was attended by about 100 supporters who heard comments from residents whose lives have been impacted by data centers and power lines and from state legislators supporting plans to halt work on new projects until new regulations to limit those impacts can be established. The event was held a week after Sen. Russet Perry (D-31) submitted a bill for the upcoming General Assembly session that would impose a three-year state moratorium and just days before a Board of Supervisors vote on plans to slow review of projects in Loudoun County. Jared Mummert is leading the data center reform campaign for the PEC. “For more than 26 years, data centers have been a part of life here in Loudoun, and there is no community that understands and has seen the transition of this industry like us,” he said in kicking off the rally. “We have seen this industry turn from smaller centers closer to office parks … and they have transitioned into energy-guzzling, grid-destabilizing, water-consuming, ear-ringing, air-polluting, skyrocketing electric bill giants that they are today. And they're ugly, absolutely.” “Loudoun has 233 data centers, with 100 more on the way, and there are hundreds of others across the state. Today, from the data center capital of the world, we say enough is enough,” Mummert said. Speakers included Ashley Warmerling, a Lovettsville area resident leading the fight against the Valley North transmission line; Victor Block, the HOA president working to limit the impact of new transmission lines on his Loudoun Valley Estates neighborhood; Gregory Pirio, a Sterling resident who raised concerns about the health impacts of a natural gas power plant feeding a data center in his community; Sarina Virmani, a Riverside High School student working to help young people have a greater voice in community issues; and attorney Phillip Thompson, a member of the Loudoun NAACP who said a moratorium is needed to protect the public’s health and safety. Perry and Del. John McAuliff (D-30) said they will continue to make better regulations of data centers a top priority. “When I first ran for office last year, I channeled, or I tried to channel the best I could, that anger and that frustration into the first race ever fully focused on data centers, and we won—with your help, we won,” McAuliff said. “This year, you've shown up at public hearings, raised your concerns, and asked whether anybody is listening while project after project continues to move forward. No more. Because of your voice, our leaders in Richmond, governors, senators, congressmen from around the country are all racing to show how much they're going to do about data centers because of the work that you all have done.” McAuliff said history was made last year when the General Assembly imposed the first restrictions on dirty diesel generators and the first zoning rules on data centers. “No one had ever done that before until you spoke up,” he said. McAuliff laid out a five-point plan for additional work to better protect the region. That includes ending the use of dirty diesel generators for all existing data centers, banning data centers in low groundwater areas and on farmland, making existing data centers pay for “every dime” of their energy and infrastructure need, protecting homes and farms from transmission lines and fully compensate those impacted, and imposing a moratorium on new data center development across the commonwealth. “You have done your part by showing up today, making your voices heard time and time again. It is now our responsibility to take those concerns and turn them into actions,” McAuliff said. “Don't stop speaking up. Don't stop organizing. … We have already sent an unmistakable message, which is that we demand better and we will win.” Perry said that when she first went to Richmond three years ago, the state senators who were concerned about the impacts of data centers could fit inside a Honda Civic. But that has changed. “[There were] three of us, three of 40. It was worse than apathy,” she said. “Just last year, Governor Youngkin stood before the General Assembly and delivered his State of the Commonwealth address. And what he said was he wanted Virginia to be the data center capital of the world, and the room jumped to its feet, including people who represent Loudoun County. Rest assured, I was not clapping, and I certainly was not standing. But things have changed, and you all are all the reasons.” State leaders are increasingly raising concerns about higher electric bills, groundwater depletion, the loss of farmland and community impacts of data centers and transmission lines. “Legislators from across the commonwealth are slowly, too slowly, but starting to join and see what you all have been saying for so long,” Perry said. “Virginia does not exist to be a pass-through state for corporate greed. We do not exist to swallow massive high-voltage lines and bail out bad corporate math. And we will not be quieted. The project is Times Digital’s first market-oriented overseas benchmark project, marking the formal export of its new-energy technical service capabilities. MAS is located in Ha’il province, about 590 km north of Riyadh, and is a key independent power producer project under Round 5 of Saudi Arabia’s National Renewable Energy Program, developed by a consortium of EDF, SPIC Yellow River Hydropower and Saudi SAPCO. The project is scheduled to begin pre-energization commissioning on November 15 and achieve partial grid connection by the end of November; once fully operational, it is expected to generate 4.4 billion kWh annually. Times Digital’s domestic new-energy O&M service portfolio has exceeded 34 GW.

artigo.texto: Teles questionam obrigação de investir em data centers no leilão para expansão da telefonia móvel Operadoras defenderam que os recursos sejam direcionados prioritariamente à ampliação da cobertura e à melhoria da qualidade dos serviços de telecomunicações A Telefônica Brasil, dona da Vivo, e a Claro questionaram a proposta da Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações (Anatel) de incluir investimentos em data centers entre os compromissos previstos para as empresas vencedoras do futuro leilão de frequências destinadas à expansão da telefonia móvel, na porção superior da faixa de 6 Ghz. Em audiência pública nesta sexta-feira (16), as operadoras defenderam que os recursos sejam direcionados prioritariamente à ampliação da cobertura e à melhoria da qualidade dos serviços de telecomunicações. Confira os resultados e indicadores da Telefônica Brasil e das demais companhias de capital aberto no portal Valor Empresas 360 Além dos compromissos de expansão da cobertura móvel e de implantação de redes de transporte de dados, o edital contempla investimentos destinados à implantação de data centers nas regiões Norte, Nordeste e Centro-Oeste, com o objetivo de ampliar a infraestrutura de processamento e interconexão de dados nessas localidades. O modelo segue a lógica adotada em leilões recentes de frequências, nos quais as empresas vencedoras assumem compromissos de investimento em contrapartida à autorização para explorar as faixas. Durante a audiência, o representante da Telefônica, Raphael Andrade, afirmou que a empresa reconhece a relevância dos data centers para o desenvolvimento do ecossistema digital brasileiro, mas ressaltou que esse tipo de investimento não está previsto no decreto que estabelece as políticas públicas de telecomunicações e delimita as modalidades de compromissos que podem ser previstas em leilões. "Observa-se que experiências internacionais para a construção desse tipo de infraestrutura, especialmente na Europa, têm sido estruturadas predominantemente por meio de modelos de investimento público-privado", disse. "A Telefônica considera acertado que a futura licitação dos 6 GHz preserve caráter não arrecadatório, mas com a previsão de compromissos de investimentos aderentes à expansão da conectividade." Pela Claro, Monique Barros também questionou a inclusão de data centers entre as obrigações previstas no edital. Segundo ela, embora essas estruturas sejam importantes para a transformação digital, os investimentos exigidos das vencedoras deveriam estar diretamente relacionados à ampliação da cobertura, da capacidade e da qualidade das redes móveis. "A questão que colocamos para reflexão não é sobre a importância do data center, e sim se a sua implementação deve constituir compromisso vinculado à aquisição de espectro, destinado às redes móveis e financiado pelas vencedoras do leilão", afirmou. "O setor de telecom já tem muitos desafios em si, não só por ser capital intensivo, mas também por ter altíssimo grau de competição, necessidade de contínua evolução tecnológica, baixa rentabilidade e, em especial, enfrenta muitas limitações econômicas da população brasileira." Expansão da cobertura de telefonia móvel A faixa de 6 GHz é considerada estratégica para a expansão da capacidade das redes de telefonia móvel e para a evolução das tecnologias de comunicação. A expectativa é que essas frequências possam ser utilizadas para aprimorar os serviços de 5G, inclusive com a tecnologia 5G Advanced, que permite melhorias de velocidade, capacidade e desempenho das redes, e, futuramente, viabilizar a implantação do 6G. O futuro leilão também prevê compromissos de ampliação da cobertura de telefonia móvel em localidades atualmente desatendidas, com exigência mínima de tecnologia 4G. As empresas vencedoras poderão, no entanto, optar pela implantação de redes 5G nessas áreas. Segundo dados da Anatel, 24.936 localidades brasileiras ainda não possuem cobertura de telefonia móvel, de um total de 58.404 localidades consideradas no levantamento, atualizado em outubro de 2026. Apesar disso, segundo a agência, 93,74% da população brasileira vivem em localidades que possuem cobertura do serviço. A agência aponta que cerca de 9 mil localidades estão contempladas em compromissos já assumidos pelas prestadoras para atendimento escalonado até 2030. A agência, no entanto, ainda não tem uma estimativa de quantas localidades poderão ser beneficiadas pelos compromissos de cobertura previstos no futuro leilão da faixa de 6 GHz. Segundo a Anatel, essa definição depende do cálculo do valor das frequências que serão licitadas, etapa que permitirá dimensionar os investimentos associados ao certame. A relação de localidades que poderão receber investimentos também será atualizada mais perto da publicação do edital, considerando eventuais mudanças na cobertura existente até lá. Cronograma A proposta da Anatel, atualmente em consulta pública, prevê a realização do leilão da faixa de 6 GHz até 2028, mas as operadoras também questionam o cronograma previsto pela agência reguladora. O prazo para apresentação de contribuições à proposta termina na próxima sexta-feira (23). Após essa etapa, as sugestões serão analisadas pela área técnica da agência, e o edital voltará à avaliação do Conselho Diretor da Anatel antes de sua aprovação definitiva. O representante da Telefônica defendeu a realização do leilão após 2030, quando estarão concluídos os compromissos de investimento assumidos pelas empresas no leilão do 5G, realizado em 2021. BYD Energy Storage operates nine O&M centers globally, each spanning 2,500 square meters. Its after-sales service network covers China, Chile, South Africa, the UK, the US, Australia, Japan, Poland, and the Middle East. New service centers will open in South Africa and Bulgaria in 2027 to further expand its global service footprint. The centers deliver core functions including spare parts storage and management, batteries repair and maintenance, regional spare parts allocation, batteries recycling, and training for locally hired engineers. BYD Energy Storages regional centers fully comply with local regulatory requirements, deliver structured workforce training and enable rapid on-site response. The professional service team comprises over 200 field engineers and more than 100 R&D specialists. The company enforces standardized service SLAs: response within 24 hours, on-site arrival within 48 hours, and fault troubleshooting within 7 days. The company’s global service network has achieved widespread coverage. It forms a multi-point supply network that ensures rapid spare parts delivery worldwide. Furthermore, leveraging localized production lines, its O&M teams integrate regional resources to deliver local battery repair services, providing global customers with fast, convenient, and localized after-sales support. Our global service footprint is tailored to our fastgrowing BESS deployments. Trustworthy aftersales support underpins the longterm stable operation of energy storage assets, commented Mr. He Dehong, Head of Global After-sales Service at BYD Energy Storage. Guided by its vision, empower global energy storage industry with digital and intelligent service, BYD Energy Storages mature global O&M system strongly supports its expanding battery energy storage footprint. The company topped global BESS shipments at over 60 GWh in 2025, and has delivered more than 650 energy storage projects in total, supported by standardized, localized after-sales services for reliable asset operation. artigo.texto: POWERGRID Invites Bids for 187.5 MW/750 MWh Battery Storage Project 19 Oct 2026 2 Min Read CW Team Share Power Grid Corporation of India (POWERGRID) has invited online bids for developing a 187.5 MW/750 MWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) in Telangana. The project is intended to strengthen grid stability and support the integration of renewable energy into the electricity network. Designated as Package TS-BESS-01, the project carries Tender Reference Number CC/T/W-BESS/DOM/A02/26/14098. The proposed BESS will provide 187.5 MW of power capacity and 750 MWh of energy storage, equivalent to 4 hours of storage at full output. The tender is being conducted through the Tariff Based Competitive Bidding (TBCB) route and is classified as a power and energy project works contract. Eligible companies can access the tender documents through POWERGRID’s PRANIT Portal using RFX Number 5002005732, subject to the stated technical, financial and pre-qualification requirements. The participation fee has been fixed at Rs. 25,000, while the tender value and earnest money deposit (EMD) are listed as zero on the portal. Bidders are required to review the official documents for eligibility conditions, technical specifications, commercial requirements and other instructions before submitting their offers. The tender schedule set October 12, 2026, at 7:50 PM as the start of document sales and soft copy bid submissions. Document sales will close on October 17 at 11:55 PM, while bids must be submitted by October 19 at 11:00 AM and are scheduled to be opened at 11:30 AM the same day. The tender is being managed by Satyam Gupta, Engineer (CS), from POWERGRID’s corporate office in Gurugram, Haryana. The project will add flexible storage capacity that can absorb electricity when supply is available and discharge it during periods of higher demand or lower renewable generation, supporting grid balancing and the wider integration of solar and wind power. artigo.texto: A factory in Guadalajara, Mexico, had incorporated solar panels, but still faced a problem that conditioned its activity: micro-power outages forced the welding machines and other equipment to stop, interrupting processes that could not always be resumed immediately. The solution required approximately four months of pre-engineering and culminated, in August 2026, with the installation of a 150 kW power and 261 kWh capacity BESS system, designed to provide backup in the event of supply interruptions. However, behind that decision was a question that went beyond the needs of a single factory: how to determine if an investment in energy storage is profitable for an industry or business, and what factors should be considered before incorporating batteries . In that sense, for Sergio Rodríguez , Director of Technology for LATAM at Solis for Latin America, during the program"It Had to Be Said and It Was Said " on Energía Estratégica , the value of these solutions does not depend solely on how much electricity they can store, but also on the operational characteristics of the client, the tariff charges and the economic consequences of an interruption. “Investing in storage is not an expense, but a long-term investment that, as a company, makes me more competitive and much more reliable in my daily production,” he stated. The calculation that determines the profitability of a BESS According to the executive, conventional photovoltaic projects can achieve investment recovery periods of between two and three years , while those installations that incorporate storage can have periods of five to six years . However, he clarified that these values change according to the characteristics of each operation, especially when the costs derived from power outages are incorporated. In certain industrial processes, a power outage of just one hour can compromise practically an entire day of production, due to the time required to restart the facilities. "You practically lose a day because of a power outage of maybe an hour," he exemplified. But energy backup is not the only variable that can justify the investment. The specialist identified two additional applications: load shifting and peak shaving , which are especially relevant for companies subject to time-differentiated tariffs or charges associated with contracted power. In these cases, batteries allow electricity to be stored when it is available at a lower cost and used later, or to reduce the maximum demand recorded by an installation. Cost trends are also altering the economic conditions of these projects. According to a survey by the Brazilian consulting firm Greener , the implementation cost of BESS systems between 500 and 1000 kWh fell by 53% between 2020 and 2025 , dropping from 3.97 to 1.88 reais per Wh. The firm estimates a cost of 1.73 reais per Wh by 2026. Commercial expansion accompanies this trend. In Brazil, manufacturers and suppliers registered orders for 730 MWh of storage in 2025 , a volume equivalent to that sold during the previous five years. Between January and March 2026 alone, another 504 MWh were added, reaching approximately 1.9 GWh of systems sold or contracted . Although these figures cover different applications and do not exclusively represent commercial and industrial installations, they show the acceleration of a market in which the costs of technology are beginning to facilitate new business models. Which sectors are driving consultations in Latin America? Demand also shows significant differences between countries and economic activities. In Mexico , Solis identifies inquiries coming from metallurgical industries, aluminum manufacturers, supermarkets, and small and medium-sized enterprises. In Chile and Peru , one of the main sectors interested is mining, while in Argentina Rodríguez highlighted the potential of the agro-industry. In the Dominican Republic, opportunities are emerging related to small businesses that require smaller-scale backup solutions. Bolivia, meanwhile, is registering increased interest in photovoltaic energy combined with storage in a context of energy supply difficulties. According to the executive, Chile is currently Solis's largest sales volume market in C&I storage , although Mexico also presents significant opportunities due to the diversity of industrial applications. This growth finds potential support in the expansion of distributed generation. In Mexico, statistics from the National Energy Commission (CNE) recorded 5,164.98 MW of distributed photovoltaic capacity at the end of 2025 , associated with 600,368 applications processed. Jalisco, the state where the Guadalajara project was developed, led the national deployment of distributed generation with 747.67 MW and 99,949 applications , considering the set of technologies registered under that scheme. Engineering, a prerequisite for the business to function Rodríguez emphasized that profitability is also conditioned by the size and selection of the equipment. A company that needs backup during micro-outages does not necessarily require the same solution as another interested in shifting several hours of electricity consumption. For this reason, Solis is committed to hybrid systems and modular architectures that allow capacity to be adjusted to the characteristics of each establishment, from small commercial facilities to larger projects. The company also identifies opportunities for solutions that can reach approximately 15 MW of power through modular configurations , approaching the boundary between the C&I segment and larger-scale applications. However, the executive argued that technology selection should begin with an analysis of customer needs and not solely with the product offer. This stage involves manufacturers, distributors, EPC companies and integrators, whose participation allows defining the electrical characteristics, installation and commissioning. artigo.texto: (Xinhua/Guo Qi) Fuzhou, 16 out (Xinhua) — A Conferência Mundial de Armazenamento de Energia 2026 acontece de quarta a sexta-feira na cidade de Ningde, na Província de Fujian, no leste da China, reunindo participantes para discutir tecnologias de ponta, perspectivas para o setor de armazenamento de energia e a posição da China no mercado global de armazenamento de energia. Em 2025, as adições anuais globais de armazenamento em baterias atingiram aproximadamente 307 GWh, sendo que a China respondeu por 56%. A escala de implantação na China tornou-se fundamental para o mercado global de armazenamento e está “ajudando a mudar a economia da eletricidade renovável”, disse Ilina Stefanova, chefe da Coalizão para Ação da Agência Internacional de Energia Renovável (IRENA), na cerimônia de abertura. A experiência da China em tecnologia, fabricação, implantação e integração à rede será importante não apenas no âmbito nacional, mas também para a transição energética global, acrescentou ela. À medida que as energias renováveis se tornam uma importante fonte de energia em todo o mundo, o armazenamento está evoluindo de uma instalação de apoio para uma nova infraestrutura essencial para os sistemas de energia. É preciso atender às diversas demandas da rede elétrica e, ao mesmo tempo, melhorar continuamente a confiabilidade e a estabilidade, disse Zeng Yuqun, fundador e presidente da CATL, fabricante líder de baterias da China, com sede na cidade de Ningde. Dados do setor mostram que a China está respondendo a essas demandas. O setor de armazenamento de energia de novo tipo da China alcançou resultados notáveis, disse Xiong Jijun, vice-ministro da Indústria e Informatização, em seu discurso de abertura. A produção de baterias de armazenamento da China ultrapassou 420 GWh no primeiro semestre de 2026, um aumento anual de cerca de 110%. O setor está avançando por diversas vias tecnológicas, com as baterias de lítio desempenhando um papel de liderança ao lado das baterias de íons de sódio e de fluxo. O governo buscará equilibrar desenvolvimento e segurança, fortalecerá a inovação tecnológica, seguirá princípios orientados pela demanda e promoverá um ecossistema industrial global, ao mesmo tempo que se protegerá firmemente contra a competição desenfreada e orientará o setor para que passe da expansão em escala para um crescimento impulsionado pela inovação, acrescentou Xiong. A cidade de Ningde já sediou a conferência três vezes anteriormente, um evento que atraiu representantes de governos, indústrias e da academia de mais de 50 países e regiões. artigo.texto: A obrigação de investir em data centers na venda da faixa de 6Ghz foi questionada pela Claro e pela Vivo, na audiência pública realizada pela Anatel, nesta sexta-feira, 16/10, em Brasília. A proposta em consulta prevê financiar núcleos regionais neutros e nós de borda, com prioridade para áreas menos atendidas por esse tipo de infraestrutura. Os recursos seriam aportados pelas vencedoras e administrados por uma entidade constituída por elas, sob a governança de um grupo presidido pela Anatel. “A questão não é sobre a importância do data center, e sim se a sua implementação deve constituir compromisso vinculado à aquisição de espectro”, declarou a representante da Claro, Monique Barros. A tele destacou que a Anatel acertou em destinar a maior parte da faixa para as teles. Lembrou que a maturidade de equipamentos era essencial para definir o leilão de 6gHz e não há um ecossistema robusto para a frequência. Lembrou que no leilão do 5G, quando se vendeu a faixa de 26GHz, e até hoje, não há ecossistema para o melhor uso da faixa. A Claro diz que é preciso refletir se a implantação de data centers têm de ser obrigatoriedade de edital de licitação, mesmo reconhecendo a relevância deles para o ambiente digital. A Claro quer manter os investimentos na ampliação da conectividade. A operadora também pediu a prorrogação da audiência pública, em análise pelo Conselho Diretor da Agência. A Anatel admite que incluir data centers é uma novidade e diz que é preciso abrir o olhar para outros investimentos em infraestrutura digital, mesmo tendo ainda lacunas em conectividade. A implantação de data centers não é prevista nas politicas públicas de telecomunicações e não pode ser vinculada à liberação de espectro, afirmou o representante da Vivo, Rafael Andrade de Oliveira. A operadora disse que a Anatel acertou em destinar a parte maior do espectro para as operadoras de telecomunicações, mas disse que a licitação só deveria acontecer depois de 2030. A operadora também disse que é desnecessária ter uma entidade administradora.

artigo.texto: Colorado startup recognized for its anode-free sodium-ion cell and safe, liquid electrolyte platform DETROIT, Oct. 16, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Mana Battery, Inc., a Colorado-based developer of high-energy, anode-free sodium-ion battery technology, today announced that it has received the Battery Innovation of the Year award at The Battery Show North America 2026, held October 12-15 in Detroit. The Battery Awards, presented live at the show and judged by members of its conference advisory board, recognize innovation, excellence and leadership across the battery and electric vehicle industry. The award recognizes Mana Battery's anode-free sodium ion battery cell and enabling liquid electrolyte technology: a proprietary cell architecture that is assembled without anode active material, with the sodium anode forming in place during charging. The design removes a costly component while delivering energy density beyond lithium iron phosphate (LFP). Sodium chemistry also relies on abundant, domestically available materials. "This award is a result of years-long efforts across R&D, cell engineering, materials scaling, and commercial validation. Starting with work by Professor Chunmei Ban and Mana CTO Nick Singstock at CU Boulder, and now being carried forward by an incredible group of engineers, scientists, and operators at Mana, this award belongs to a team that set out to prove that sodium-ion can be denser, and safer, than the incumbent chemistries, not just cheaper," said Tyler Evans, co-founder and CEO of Mana Battery. "Recognition by the industry at The Battery Show tells us the market is ready for what we are building." "Our liquid electrolyte is the foundation of everything we do," said Nick Singstock, co-founder and CTO of Mana Battery. "It is what makes a stable, high-energy anode-free sodium cell possible, and it is designed from the molecule up to improve safety and performance." Mana is scaling its anode-free sodium-ion cell through partnership with established battery manufacturers. Along the way, Mana is selling sodium-ion electrolytes as a stand-alone product to battery manufacturers for sodium-ion cells with a hard carbon anode. The recognition follows a year of commercial and technical progress. In August 2026, Mana Battery signed a Joint Development Agreement with Saft, a TotalEnergies subsidiary, to co-develop and commercialize anode-free sodium-ion cells for defense and other markets. Since then, it has signed a second Joint Development Agreement with a global leader in the production of EV’s and ESS. Mana's technology has been advanced through government-funded programs including grants from ARPA-E, the U.S. Army and the NSF. The company is sampling cells and electrolyte to multiple commercial partners, alongside 14 projects with customers including funded Material Transfer Agreements and Cell Testing Agreements. About Mana Battery Mana Battery, Inc. is a battery technology company based in Broomfield, Colorado, developing high-energy sodium-ion batteries on a proprietary electrolyte platform and anode-free cell architecture. Founded in 2023 as a spin-out of the University of Colorado Boulder, the company targets defense, grid energy storage, data center and electric vehicle applications with batteries that pair safe liquid electrolyte with a supply chain free of critical-mineral constraints. Learn more at manabattery.us. Media Contact Sam Jaffe · VP, Business Development and Product, Mana Battery, Inc. · [email protected] · +1 (303) 502-4001

artigo.texto: BYD takes ultra-fast charging overseas for the first time, rolling out a network in Indonesia - Input - 2026-10-19 10:07:59 - Updated - 2026-10-19 10:07:59 [Financial News] BYD Company Limited (BYD), a Chinese electric vehicle maker, is expanding into overseas markets for ultra-fast charging infrastructure, starting with Indonesia. It plans to build a charging network using its self-developed flash-charging technology and also launched premium electric vehicles equipped with its second-generation BYD Blade Battery. The strategy is to expand its business model overseas, combining electric vehicle sales with batteries and charging infrastructure. BYD said on the 19th that it announced plans to build a flash-charging network in Indonesia on the 14th and launched the new D9 and Z9GT from its premium brand Denza. This is the first time BYD’s flash-charging technology has entered an overseas market. BYD plans to first install flash chargers at 10 Denza showrooms in Indonesia so customers can try them out, and to gradually expand the public charging network starting at year-end. The flash charger is distinguished by its integration with an energy storage system (ESS). BYD was the first in the world to apply a T-shaped suspended design. It also improved convenience by introducing a “Zero Gravity” charger that reduces the burden of the charging cable’s weight, and a Plug and Charge function that enables charging authentication and payment simply by connecting the vehicle. Alongside expanding its charging infrastructure, BYD also strengthened its new-car lineup. The new Denza D9, a luxury multipurpose vehicle (MPV), is the first model to feature the second-generation BYD Blade Battery and flash-charging technology. It targets families and business customers with improved driving range, powertrain performance and ride comfort. The Denza Z9GT, launched alongside it, is a luxury electric vehicle combining high-performance driving with intelligent control technology, built on a dedicated e3 platform. BYD aims to expand its foothold in Indonesia’s premium eco-friendly vehicle market with the two models. Liu Xueliang, vice president of BYD Group and general manager of its Asia-Pacific Automotive Business Unit, said, “BYD’s technological innovation has gone beyond simply making and selling cars.” He added, “I believe technological innovation can create greater value for society and bring the benefits of advanced technology to more people.” [email protected] Kim Dong-ho Reporter

artigo.texto: Hunterbrook Media’s investment affiliate, Hunterbrook Capital, does not have any positions related to this article at the time of publication. Positions may change at any time. Full disclosures below. This is the latest investigation in Hunterbrook Media’s series on the poisoning of American communities. For decades, polluters have released toxins across the U.S. We've built a nationwide database to expose harm to communities and ecosystems, then hold accountable those responsible. After reporting from Illinois, Nebraska, California, Texas, Louisiana, New Mexico, Indiana, and Virginia, this investigation takes us to Hawaii. Hunterbrook Media has also investigated environmental damage spanning from Namibia to Argentina to Peru. Please email ideas@hntrbrk.com if you suspect pollution or poisoning in your community. In 2025, Digital Realty spent $120 million to purchase a 97-acre parcel of land that was once part of Fort Gillem, a former United States Army post in Forest Park, Georgia. The company, one of the world’s largest real estate investment trusts, is constructing a massive data center complex on the site, returning valuable land to a “productive, tax-generating use,” as its executives put it. But the land came with a historical burden. From 1941 until around 1980 the Army dumped everything from gas masks and medical waste to solvents and sewage sludge on this parcel in the northwest corner of the former army base that now houses a maze of warehouses, including a Kroger distribution center and an Amazon delivery station. There’s quite a bit of environmental issues with the site,” a Digital Realty asset manager said at a meeting with county officials in 2025. “Tons and tons and tons of — physical tons — of trash and environmental hazards.” An investigation by Hunterbrook found that the hazards unearthed included military waste that was still combustible. Meanwhile, residents in neighboring communities are reporting cracks on their walls from explosive blasting on the site and say their questions about environmental and health threats stemming from Digital Realty’s Fort Gillem project are being ignored. The company plans to spend $3 billion on this project, and the first phase is expected to open in early 2028. But a document filed with the Georgia Environmental Protection Division suggests construction may surface some surprises. In December 2025, the company encountered white phosphorus on the property, which “reacted when exposed to air and exhibited a dense white smoke,” according to a letter an environmental consultant sent on behalf of Digital Realty to Georgia EPD. The company asked the Army for guidance and contacted the local police department, which sent a bomb squad to inspect and sample the material. The letter states that the white phosphorus was found in an area on the western side of the property that’s going to be under the planned data center. “Upon completion of the Property’s redevelopment, the area of concern will be encapsulated with a concrete building foundation,” the letter states. “At this time, the size of the area of concern is not known but is not anticipated to be larger than 100-feet by 100-feet by 8-feet deep based on grading already completed at the Property.” The material has since been removed, a Digital Realty spokesperson told Hunterbrook in an email. “Trained professionals carefully excavated the 100-foot by 100-foot by 8-foot area in accordance with an approved work plan, using appropriate equipment and personal protective equipment to identify any additional material containing white phosphorus,” the spokesperson wrote. “The excavation recovered five 30-gallon steel drums of material containing white phosphorus, far less than could have been encountered across the full area. The drums were then transported under a hazardous waste manifest to a permitted treatment, storage, and disposal facility.” The company also said that “work in the area where the material was initially discovered was stopped immediately upon the discovery of the material” and that “there were no reported injuries.” No other munitions and explosives of concern have been encountered since the white phosphorus discovery, according to Digital Realty. A Georgia EPD spokesperson confirmed the temporary work stoppage in the area where white phosphorus was found and that Digital Realty was in the process of removing the material in February, when EPD representatives visited the site. White phosphorus is used in artillery shells, rockets, and grenades to create dense smoke screens, provide battlefield illumination, mark targets, or act as an incendiary weapon. The use of white phosphorus weapons in civilian areas has been considered a war crime by human rights organizations like Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International. Its presence at the Digital Realty construction site “is assumed to be associated with historical Army disposal operations,” according to the letter to the Georgia EPD. “Measures are in place to protect construction workers, future occupants, and the public throughout remediation and development activities,” the Digital Realty spokesperson told Hunterbrook. Toxic Land Is Data Center Boom’s Next Frontier The frenzied AI build-out has turned Digital Realty into a digital infrastructure colossus. According to its website, Digital Realty operates more than 300 data centers worldwide. It counts Oracle, IBM, Meta, AT&T, JPMorgan Chase & Co. and Morgan Stanley among its customers. Amid the scramble to feed AI’s seemingly endless need for compute, other companies besides Digital Realty have resorted to building data centers on contaminated land. TeraWulf is developing the former Century Aluminum smelter site in Hawesville, Kentucky, into a more than $4 billion data center campus, with Anthropic as its tenant.
