artigo.texto: A $200 million loan, a carbon-credit market, and a Rayong industrial platform aim to cut energy costs, draw in private capital, and create jobs, officials say. Thailand’s Ministry of Finance and the World Bank Group have unveiled a suite of initiatives designed to finance clean energy, build a credible carbon market, and crowd in private investment, as the 2026 IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings drew to a close in Bangkok. Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas and World Bank Group President Ajay Banga announced the measures on Saturday (October 17) under the theme "Low Carbon Cities and Energy Security: Building Systems at Scale, Mobilising Private Capital, Creating Jobs". At the heart of the plan is the Low Carbon Cities and Carbon Market Development Project (LCC). The initiative aims to facilitate transparent, verifiable carbon-credit transactions aligned with international standards, supporting Thailand's commitments under the Paris Agreement and its national net-zero targets. To kick-start the project, the World Bank is providing a $200 million loan to the Export-Import Bank of Thailand (EXIM Thailand), backed by a sovereign guarantee from the Ministry of Finance. The funds will enable energy service companies (ESCOs) to invest in clean energy and energy efficiency across public-sector assets, preparing both public and private sectors for evolving market standards. Ekniti also highlighted a $2.4 million World Bank grant under the Partnership for Market Implementation, alongside contributions from Krung Thai Bank (KTB), to establish the framework for a just transition. KTB will play a central role in aggregating, verifying, and monetising greenhouse gas emission reductions to connect credits with domestic and international buyers. The strategy spans three main pillars of cooperation: • Business Transition: KTB and the Department of Climate Change and Environment (DCCE) will develop financial tools to help small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) transition to low-carbon technologies while supporting affected workers. • Carbon-Credit Market: KTB will aggregate credits, while the Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET) establishes a transparent auction and price-discovery mechanism. Prospective buyers including Grab, ACEIS Electric and Power, DriverAI, and Thai Airways have expressed interest. All credits must complete formal validation and verification prior to sale. • Industrial Investment: PTT, KTB, and the DCCE will create blended-finance mechanisms for the I-SPARK low-carbon industrial platform in the Map Ta Phut–Rayong area, aiming to mobilise private capital for speciality, bio-based, and circular industries. Ekniti stressed that development finance must be measured by outcomes rather than capital raised. Over time, he noted, robust carbon markets and accessible green financing should reduce Thailand's reliance on government subsidies and tax incentives. He acknowledged that the government must deliver clear regulatory frameworks and bankable projects to accelerate scale. "Success should be measured by whether we can bring down energy costs, make industry more competitive, and create better jobs. That should be the legacy of the Annual Meetings 2026," Ekniti said, requesting further guarantee support from the World Bank and the International Finance Corporation (IFC). Commending Thailand for its exceptional hospitality throughout the summit, Banga emphasised that the success of the carbon framework hinges entirely on credibility. "Without trust and credibility, nothing would happen," Banga noted, pointing to the partnership between the SET, the Securities and Exchange Commission, and KTB as the "secret sauce" that will attract private investors. Banga outlined three key advantages of the initiative: 1. Cost Savings: Energy efficiency reduces utility bills for businesses, cities, and households, freeing up public funds for schools, roads, and services while creating local maintenance jobs. 2. Private Capital Integration: Government budgets alone cannot fund modern infrastructure. "There is not enough public money to do these kinds of things," Banga said, stressing that private capital is essential to scale impact. 3. Market Continuity: A thriving commercial ecosystem ensures businesses continue investing in urban sustainability without permanent reliance on public funding. According to government officials, the initiatives align with a broader strategy to use finance as a tool for economic restructuring. By addressing market constraints and establishing reliable financial data, the public sector aims to de-risk green investments for institutional capital.

artigo.texto: LS Electric has signed a contract worth approximately 170 billion won to supply switchgear for artificial intelligence (AI) data centers operated by a major US technology company. The company has secured supply volumes for 2027 and is negotiating additional orders for 2028, along with other power equipment. LS Electric announced on Oct. 19 that it had signed a long-term agreement (LTA) worth $125.23 million to supply power distribution solutions for North American data centers. The customer was not identified because of a confidentiality agreement. The contract covers a two-year period from 2027 to 2028. The announced contract value represents deliveries scheduled for 2027, while the volume for 2028 will be determined through further negotiations with the customer. The products covered by the agreement are 38-kilovolt (kV) high-voltage switchgear systems. Switchgear distributes incoming high-voltage electricity to equipment throughout a data center and protects facilities in the event of electrical faults. LS Electric is also discussing additional supplies of low-voltage switchgear, distribution transformers and high-voltage ring main units (RMUs). The company is expanding its US operations through LS Electric Utah in Cedar City, Utah, and its Bastrop Campus in Texas. It has established local capabilities covering sales, engineering, manufacturing and services to meet demand from North American data center customers. “We will expand supplies of high-value-added power equipment for data centers to secure a stable revenue base and improve profitability,” an LS Electric official said.

The importance of stable power supply and energy storage is increasing as AI data centers' power demand rises and renewable energy generation expands. Progress toward commercializing solid-state batteries is also encouraging. Samsung SDI is pursuing technology development and collaboration with customers with the goal of mass-producing solid-state batteries in 2027, while domestic materials companies are working to secure production capacity for key raw materials. The government also plans to provide about KRW 400 billion in research and development support for next-generation batteries over five years starting in 2027. The SOL Solid State Battery&Silicon Anode Materials ETF responds to these industry shifts by concentrating its investments in key companies involved in solid-state batteries and silicon anode materials. Its major holdings include Samsung SDI, which is working toward mass production of solid-state batteries; LG Energy Solution, a key ESS company; EcoPro BM, a solid-state battery cathode material company; Isu Specialty Chemical, a company involved in lithium sulfide; LOTTE Energy Materials, a battery materials company; and Daejoo Electronic Materials, a silicon anode material company. artigo.texto: SK On Holds Future Technology Institute Symposium to Share Next-Generation Battery Research Achievements Research Team Wins Grand Prize for Improving LFP Cathode Manufacturing Process More Than 300 Research Projects Submitted Across Six Battery Fields Sharing Research Achievements and Strengthening Technological Competitiveness SK On said on October 18 that it had held the 2nd Future Technology Institute Symposium to share research achievements in next-generation battery technologies. The event was held for two days starting October 14 at SK On's Future Technology Institute in Yuseong-gu, Daejeon. Attendees included SK On President Lee Yongwook and Future Technology Institute Director Park Gisu. Under the theme "The Future We Create," the symposium featured more than 300 research projects across six fields: battery processes, cells, systems, materials, next-generation technologies, and platforms, about 15% more than last year. This year's grand prize went to a research team that developed a process to replace expensive carbon nanotube (CNT) paste used in manufacturing lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cathodes with powder. CNTs are a material used as a conductive additive to facilitate the movement of electrons within battery electrodes. The team was recognized for uniformly dispersing CNT powder in cathode materials to achieve performance on par with existing processes while improving cost competitiveness. SK On plans to review the technology's application in actual production processes. Research on the design of electrodes for large-area pouch-type lithium-metal batteries received the top excellence award, while research on developing a model to predict capacity degradation and internal resistance based on battery charging, discharging, and storage conditions received an excellence award. The event also featured a technology exhibition showcasing key research projects. In his keynote address, Yonsei University Professor Lee Yongmin introduced the current state and outlook of digital twin technology, which recreates actual battery designs in a virtual space to analyze their performance and condition. SK On plans to make the symposium a regular event to promote knowledge exchange and research collaboration among its employees and strengthen its competitiveness in next-generation battery technologies. artigo.texto: Protests against widespread state corruption have flooded the Philippines in recent weeks, putting pressure on the leadership of a country that for years has been one of the United States’ closest military and commercial allies in Southeast Asia. The domestic turmoil threatens to shake up the U.S.-Philippines partnership, particularly given that American-funded data center projects under President Donald Trump’s Pax Silica initiative are among the targets of the protesters’ rage. On September 21, 2026, President Ferdinand Marcos — whose national trust rating sits at just 28% — put the presidential palace under lockdown in anticipation of mass protests, as more than 17,000 police officers were deployed and tens of thousands of protestors marched through Manila to demand change in the face of the country's largest corruption scandal in years. The scandal revolves around more than $9 billion worth of proposed flood-control infrastructure projects, intended for construction since Marcos took office in 2022. The projects were designed to improve infrastructure like drainage and flood control systems to mitigate the effects of typhoons common in the Philippines. These projects are under legal investigation for being of poor quality or having never been built at all. The investigation into the matter has led to the arrest of former Philippines House Speaker Martin Romualdez, a cousin and formerly close ally of Marcos, on a $118 million plunder charge. Romualdez is only one of a number of officials currently detained under suspicion of pocketing money from the project, with Interior Secretary Ombudsman Remulla alleging that co-conspirators attempted to hide the money through the purchase of houses or Romualdez’s $1 million donation to Harvard University. Another layer of controversy involves the impeachment trial of sitting Vice President Sara Duterte. A major point of contention occurred on day 34 of the trial, when it was revealed that over 30 undeclared accounts showed Duterte’s net worth to be over $3 million — almost 15 times more than her declared net worth of $209,000. The public backlash and corruption-induced chaos currently surrounding the Philippines could affect relations with the U.S. at a time when the United States is trying to counterbalance China’s expansive aims in the South China Sea. The military alliance between the United States and the Philippines dates back to the 1951 Mutual Defense Treaty, which ensures mutual protection in the event of a foreign armed attack. This pact was preceded by the 1947 Military Bases Agreement, an executive order granting the U.S. 20 years of renewable access to bases in the Philippines, and later reinforced by the 2014 Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement, which currently provides the U.S. rotational access to nine military bases in the archipelago. This continued relationship has established the Philippines as a crucial node in Washington’s foreign policy strategy in regard to China. Although the number of stationed U.S. troops has remained at a few hundred since the 1990s, U.S. military activity has increased, as evidenced by the fact that U.S. troops made up more than 10,000 of the 17,000 personnel from seven countries that participated in the Balikatan military exercises this May. Congress has also authorized up to $2.5 billion in foreign military financing for the Philippines, and up to $1 billion in loans for military sales, for fiscal year 2026. This is the highest amount that the U.S. has given to the Philippines, an increase of $500 million from the prior year. Outside of military investment, the Philippines has also emerged as an increasingly important ally for economic collaboration. The United States has shown intense interest in the Luzon Economic Corridor (LEC), a trilateral infrastructure and technology initiative by the U.S., Japan, and the Philippines. The plan invests in the construction of infrastructure across Luzon island. The scale is large relative to current investment: the Philippines received $7.8 billion in net foreign direct investment in 2025, while Luzon alone attracted over $20 billion in projects at a September investor forum. Though the project is still mostly aspirational, Marcos is largely in favor of it, having told a crowd of investors at the forum to turn LEC “from a shared vision into concrete investments and projects.” “The United States is all-in on the Luzon Economic Corridor because it's good for the Philippines and good for America," stated Lee Lipton, Washington’s ambassador to the Philippines, in response. The U.S. private sector is also supportive of the initiative, with over fifty American companies reported to be engaged in investment opportunities in the LEC, according to the Subic Bay Metropolitan Authority. Despite the apparent enthusiasm from both governments, the court of public opinion seems skeptical of the initiative, particularly because of one aspect of the LEC: the proposed Pax Silica technology center in the industry hub of New Clark City, estimated to attract between $40 and $70 billion in investment and create nearly 200,000 new jobs. During city-wide protests throughout Manila on September 21, protestors held signs attacking U.S.-backed data center projects, which are a part of the Pax Silica initiative, as a major source of grievance with Marcos' government. Pax Silica, which aims to pursue similar initiatives across more than 20 other countries, has sparked worry from many Filipinos over the risks of heavy water usage, high electricity demands, and overdependence on foreign technology and capital. "[Pax Silica] threatens to permanently lock the Philippines into having the highest power rates not just in Southeast Asia but in all of Asia,” stated the Makabayan Bloc, a left-wing Filipino party that, although it lacks much representation in the country’s government, has a strong grassroots presence, and has often led anti-U.S. sentiment across the country. artigo.texto: Anthropic assina seu primeiro contrato de data center no Canadá, em projeto de mais de US$ 7 bilhões Segundo a empresa, os canadenses utilizam o Claude em um dos níveis mais altos do mundo A Anthropic assinou seu primeiro contrato de locação de data center no Canadá, comprometendo-se a adquirir capacidade em um novo projeto avaliado em mais de US$ 7,1 bilhões na província de Nova Escócia, no leste do país. “Os canadenses utilizam o Claude em um dos níveis mais altos do mundo, e isso aproxima nossa infraestrutura das pessoas que dependem dela”, afirmou Jacob Glick, diretor de políticas públicas da Anthropic no Canadá, em comunicado publicado no LinkedIn. Mais cedo, nesta sexta-feira, a EverWind Fuels anunciou planos para construir um complexo de data centers e uma infraestrutura de geração de energia eólica na Nova Escócia, classificando o projeto como o maior investimento financiado pelo setor privado na história da província. A empresa canadense de energia limpa informou que mais de US$ 5,6 bilhões serão destinados ao desenvolvimento do data center em seu atual complexo industrial de Point Tupper, localizado a nordeste de Halifax, a capital provincial. Outros US$ 1,4 bilhão serão investidos na expansão de seu portfólio de energia eólica terrestre. “O projeto está avançando com compromissos de proteger os atuais consumidores de eletricidade contra aumentos nas tarifas, preservar os recursos hídricos locais e proporcionar benefícios duradouros à comunidade”, afirmou a EverWind em comunicado à imprensa que não identificou a Anthropic como a futura locatária. A empresa acrescentou que trabalhará com parceiros para estabelecer um programa de benefícios comunitários no valor de dezenas de milhões de dólares. A previsão é que o data center comece a operar com uma primeira fase de 95 megawatts no final de 2027, seguida por uma expansão de 325 megawatts em 2028. Quando concluído, o empreendimento terá capacidade total de 420 megawatts. A Anthropic informou a potenciais investidores que sua receita no terceiro trimestre chegou a US$ 16,8 bilhões, segundo pessoas familiarizadas com o assunto, enquanto a empresa de inteligência artificial avança em seus planos de abrir o capital. Segundo informações publicadas anteriormente pela Bloomberg, a companhia deverá começar a promover formalmente sua oferta pública inicial de ações (IPO, na sigla em inglês) já na semana de 9 de novembro. O ministro da Energia, Tim Hodgson, afirmou que o investimento no data center e na geração de energia eólica representa “um exemplo poderoso de como o potencial energético do Canadá está se concretizando — e exatamente o tipo de investimento que nosso governo vem trabalhando para atrair desde o primeiro dia”. Segundo a EverWind, o projeto deverá gerar 2.000 postos de trabalho durante as diferentes etapas da construção, além de 215 empregos permanentes na operação.

artigo.texto: The Xiaomi 18 Series is officially on its way, following its initial debut in China on September 23, 2026. Xiaomi 18 Series Launch in India: The Xiaomi 18 Series is officially on its way, following its initial debut in China on September 23, 2026. The upcoming flagship lineup introduces massive upgrades, including world-first 2nm mobile chipsets, dual 200MP camera systems, and revolutionary high-capacity silicon-anode batteries. Here is everything you need to know about what to expect from the India launch. While the series is already live in China, prominent industry insiders tip the Xiaomi 18 Series to launch in India by December 2026, matching the late-winter shopping rush. This represents an earlier launch cycle compared to previous generations, which typically arrived in India around March. The official launch events are expected to take place in the standard late-afternoon window (around 4:00 PM IST). India will likely receive the Xiaomi 18 Pro initially, while the standard Xiaomi 18 might follow in March or April 2027, and the top-tier Xiaomi 18 Pro Max might remain heavily limited or exclusive to global/China distributions. Xiaomi 18: Standard Xiaomi 18: Expected to start around ₹94,990. Xiaomi 18 Pro: Expected to retail between ₹1,29,990 and ₹1,39,990 depending on storage variants. The Silicon Battery Revolution: The standout upgrade of the 18 Series is battery density. Thanks to a new 32% silicon-anode composition, Xiaomi has packed a massive 7,000mAh battery into the Pro model without adding bulk to the body. The Pro Max pushes this boundary further with an 8,500mAh unit. Dual Display & Premium Design: The Xiaomi 18 Pro introduces a 2.7-inch secondary OLED screen on the back next to the camera module. This screen allows users to manage widgets, see incoming alerts, and use the high-quality 200MP rear camera to frame high-resolution selfies. The chassis features a premium glass-metal build protected by Xiaomi Dragon Crystal Glass 3.0. Extreme Leica Optics: Developed alongside Leica, the Pro variant boasts two massive 200MP sensors. The main lens uses a 1/1.28-inch Light Hunter 960 sensor for extreme low-light clarity, complemented by a 200MP periscope zoom lens capable of 3.2x optical telephoto macro shots. Hardware Privacy Display: Taking inspiration from secure display technologies, the 18 Pro series features a hardware-integrated privacy shield functionality, preventing side-angle snooping on your screen when you are in public areas. Next-Gen Connectivity: The devices are fully equipped for future network standards, integrating Ultra-Wideband (UWB) tracking, 5G-Advanced (5G-A), Wi-Fi 7, and Bluetooth 6.0. The series introduces the world’s first mobile platforms built on an ultra-dense 2nm architecture. Xiaomi 18 & 18 Pro: Equipped with the core Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 chipset, featuring Qualcomm's 4th-generation custom Oryon CPU architecture that hits clock speeds up to a massive 5.0GHz. Xiaomi 18 Pro Max: This top-tier model breaks away with the unthrottled Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 SoC, designed specifically to handle multi-stream 8K AI video processing and massive local generative AI large language models smoothly. All models support 100W HyperCharge wired charging (with the charging block included in the box), 50W wireless charging, and a powerful 27W reverse wireless charging capability to top up accessories or other phones on the go.

artigo.texto: OpenWorld Signs Term Sheet to Finance Solar-Powered, Distributed AI Computing Network Initially Integrated with Residential Battery Storage with Tokenized Financing Program of up to $1 Billion LAKE MARY, Fla., Oct 15, 2026 - (ACN Newswire) - OpenWorld, Inc. ("OpenWorld" or the "Company") (NASDAQ: OPNW), an innovation company advancing global real-world asset ("RWA") tokenization, today announced that it has entered into a non-binding term sheet with Meridian to establish a tokenized financing program of up to $1 billion to fund the purchase and deployment of a distributed AI computing network powered by on-site solar energy and residential battery storage. Under the term sheet, OpenWorld will serve as advisor, structuring agent and services provider for the program, and its OpenWorld Enterprise platform will finance and operate the orchestration of the network. The news follows recent OpenWorld tokenized financing announcements, including a proposed transaction to transform BeyondAI's industrial AI intellectual property rights into financeable collateral on OpenWorld's tokenization platform. Key Highlights - Meridian founded by Josh Raffaelli: Raffaelli was involved early in Tesla, Solar City, and SpaceX while at DFJ and Silver Lake. - Up to $1 billion in tokenized financing: OpenWorld structures and administers the tokenized financing program on OpenWorld Enterprise. Residential battery storage, solar panels and AI computing equipment form the asset base of the structure. - Meridian's role: Meridian holds purchase rights to Powerwall residential battery storage systems for the program and will own the storage assets within the structure. - AI inference without new data centers: AI providers pay to run trained models on the network with no new centralized data-center sites, no additional grid interconnections and no water-based cooling. The program is intended to supply capacity to one or more leading AI inference providers. - Initial deployment of 10,000 homes: Compute nodes at participating homes, with larger installations at local schools, hospitals and local commercial campuses. - Hosts get paid: Homeowners receive monthly hosting payments and lower-cost electricity, with household energy needs taking priority over computing workloads. Commercial hosts receive a share of site revenue and backup power. - Timeline: Initial installations scheduled to begin in the fourth quarter of 2026; first commercial site targeted for the first quarter of 2027. "Access to power is a major constraint on the growth of AI infrastructure," said Matt Shaw, CEO and Chairman of OpenWorld. "By bringing computing equipment to homes and commercial properties through solar generation and battery storage, we can build AI capacity closer to the power source instead of waiting years for a grid connection. Our term sheet with Meridian brings together the tokenization, financing and operating capabilities needed to develop this network at scale, and it shows what OpenWorld Enterprise is built to do: turn real-world assets into financeable, on-chain infrastructure." "Residential battery storage is the foundation of this program," said Josh Raffaelli, founder of Meridian and clean energy investor. "OpenWorld will help us finance the equipment, turning solar generation and battery storage at participating properties into infrastructure that can serve growing demand for AI computing." Solving the Power Problem in AI Infrastructure Access to power is a growing constraint on AI infrastructure. New data centers face lengthy grid interconnection timelines, local opposition and significant water demands. The planned network of home-hosted, distributed AI inference computing would place compute nodes at participating homes and larger installations at local schools, hospitals and commercial campuses, each powered by on-site solar generation and battery storage. AI providers would pay to use this computing capacity for inference, the process of running trained AI models, without requiring new centralized data-center sites, additional grid connections or water-based cooling. Participating homeowners would receive monthly hosting payments and lower-cost electricity, with household energy needs taking priority over computing workloads. Commercial hosts would receive a share of site revenue and backup power. How the Program Works Meridian, a privately held Delaware limited liability company, holds purchase rights to residential Tesla Powerwall battery storage systems for the program. The program's initial deployment is planned for 10,000 homes. Under the term sheet, OpenWorld will serve as advisor, structuring agent and services provider for the financing program. OpenWorld will establish and administer the tokenized financing structure on its OpenWorld Enterprise platform. The financing would support Meridian's purchase of residential battery storage systems, as well as the purchase by OpenWorld or a subsidiary of solar panels and associated AI computing equipment, all of which will be used within the structure. OpenWorld is also developing an integrated system to support each installation. The OpenWorld Enterprise platform will monitor equipment performance and provide investors with reporting on the underlying assets. The program is intended to supply computing capacity to one or more leading AI inference providers. Test installations are scheduled to begin in the fourth quarter of 2026, with the first commercial site targeted for the first quarter of 2027. Non-Binding Agreement The Term Sheet is non-binding, except for the provisions expressly stated to be binding, and the proposed transaction remains subject to the completion of confirmatory due diligence, negotiation and execution of definitive documentation, satisfaction of applicable conditions and completion of the contemplated transaction. artigo.texto: As operadoras Claro e Vivo manifestaram nesta sexta-feira, 16, discordância com a proposta da Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações (Anatel) de incluir investimentos em data centers regionais entre os compromissos de um futuro leilão do espectro de 6 GHz. As objeções foram levantadas em audiência pública realizada em Brasília pela agência, que tem aberta até 23 de outubro uma consulta pública sobre o edital (há pedidos para que a escuta seja prorrogada). Setorialmente, as operadoras de telecom voltaram a defender que o leilão de 6 GHz não ocorra em 2028, como atualmente prevê a Anatel. Já no que envolve os compromissos, a diretora regulatória da Claro, Monique Barros, questionou a inclusão de núcleos regionais de data center. A tele entende que apesar da infraestrutura ser complementar, as metas do leilão de 6 GHz deveriam priorizar investimentos diretamente relacionados à expansão, capacidade e qualidade da conectividade. "Ainda existem muitas oportunidades de investimentos no mercado de telecom: ampliação da cobertura em rodovias, em áreas remotas e a própria evolução tecnológica desejada com o 6 GHz. Essa evolução deveria ser o único foco dos compromissos de editais", afirmou Barros, aos técnicos da Anatel. Raphael Andrade de Oliveira, gerente sênior na área regulatória da Vivo, também levantou objeções, inclusive regulamentares. "Em que pese a relevância dos data centers, tal objetivo não se encontra entre objetivos do Decreto 9.612/2018, que dispõe sobre políticas públicas de telecomunicações e delimita as modalidades de compromissos", afirmou. O representante da Vivo também argumentou que experiências internacionais para construção desse tipo de infraestrutura têm sido estruturadas sobretudo por meio de parceria público-privadas (PPPs), e não através de obrigações vinculadas à aquisição de espectro. A proposta do edital de 6 GHz em consulta pública prevê núcleos regionais de data center e nós de borda (edge) para capacidade computacional em áreas desatendidas no Norte, Nordeste e Centro-Oeste. A infraestrutura seria custeada pelas vencedoras do leilão (por meio de uma entidade gestora) e operaria em um modelo de uso compartilhado. Tamanho dos blocos Além dos compromissos, Claro e Vivo também questionaram os blocos propostos pela Anatel na consulta. A agência sugeriu dois lotes nacionais de 200 MHz, um regional com 200 MHz (dividido em seis regiões) e outro também regional, mas com 100 MHz. Já para as empresas, o desenho ideal teria três blocos nacionais de 200 MHz (o que garantiria um lote para cada tele incumbente), acompanhado de um regional com os 100 MHz remanescentes. "Não deveria haver escassez na oferta de blocos nacionais", afirmou Raphael Andrade, da Vivo. "Na nossa visão, a estrutura que está apresentada traz potencial cenário de alta competitividade em alguns lotes e risco de lotes desertos em outros", complementou Monique Barros, da Claro.

artigo.texto: Israel wants an AI data center boom. Its power grid may not be ready The Electricity Authority is preparing new rules for connecting energy-intensive facilities as data centers could account for 20% of national electricity consumption by 2030. Industry figures say transmission bottlenecks, gas dependence and national security concerns make local computing infrastructure both a challenge and a strategic necessity. During the August 2025 heat wave, Israel broke its electricity consumption record four days in a row. The new peak of 17,282 megawatts was 10% higher than the previous record, set just two years earlier. Israel’s current electricity generation capacity stands at approximately 18,800 megawatts. Despite the strain on the system, the Electricity Authority is expected to publish a regulatory framework today for connecting data centers to the grid. The move would allow more energy-intensive facilities to connect to an electricity system already operating close to its limits during periods of peak demand. According to the Authority’s load forecast, data centers could account for up to 20% of Israel’s electricity consumption by 2030. In July, the Electricity Authority halted approvals for applications to build data centers in Israel. The framework expected today is intended as a compromise, allowing construction to proceed while limiting the strain on the country’s infrastructure. Under the proposed rules, each data center would be capped at 200 megawatts of power consumption, roughly equivalent to the electricity demand of a mid-sized Israeli city such as Rehovot or Holon. According to estimates, as many as 15 facilities could be built at the maximum capacity of 200 megawatts. The proposed cap would apply to half of the 100 connection requests submitted to Noga, Israel’s electricity system operator. According to sources in the electricity sector, generation itself will be a challenge. “Electricity generation will be a problem. We see how hard it is to build a power plant in Israel, and how much politicians try to avoid decisions like that,” they said. The transmission grid, however, poses an even greater constraint, according to the sources. “There are problems in the transmission grid in the center of the country, and so it’s actually in the periphery that the risk is an opportunity. In the Negev there is renewable energy; instead of transmitting the electricity north, you can route it to data centers.” The challenge is not only how much electricity data centers consume, but also when they consume it. “Usually, there’s a kind of balance in electricity consumption: work zones and offices during the day, and residential areas in the evening. But data centers run 24/7 and raise the base load on the system, meaning several power plants need to run without stopping,” the sources said. Heavy electricity demand would also increase consumption of natural gas from Israel’s reservoirs. According to the Energy Ministry, those reserves could be depleted in less than 20 years, and greater reliance on gas-fired generation would also increase air pollution. Why, then, do data centers need to be built in Israel? Why not rely on facilities overseas, as Israeli companies and institutions do today? “The world is in the midst of a technological arms race, in which countries and giant corporations are investing hundreds of billions of dollars in building the computing infrastructure that will determine the balance of power in the global economy in the coming decades,” Shelly Lanzman, a partner and chair of the advisory board at NED, a company specializing in building and developing data centers and the former CEO of Microsoft Israel, told Calcalist. “Already today it’s clear that the scope of computing power, its strength and its availability will be decisive factors in the ability of countries to develop technologies and preserve a competitive advantage,” she said. In this context, Lanzman argues, data centers should be treated as national infrastructure on a par with power plants, airports and communications networks. “For Israel, whose economic and security standing relies to a large extent on technological superiority, this is a national interest of the first order.” National security is another argument for operating data centers locally. Government agencies and other organizations handling sensitive information, including the Shin Bet, the Mossad, the military and hospitals, increasingly rely on advanced AI and data systems. These organizations handle information with significant security or privacy implications, making local storage an important part of protecting it. Operational independence and continuity of service are also concerns. About a year ago, Microsoft restricted Unit 8200’s access to some of its cloud services after determining that the unit had violated the company’s terms of use. The decision followed reports that the service had been used to collect information on and track Palestinians, including by storing recordings of millions of their phone calls. Beyond security, a strong domestic data center industry could give Israeli entrepreneurs an advantage when launching startups and help attract international companies. Access to computing infrastructure is becoming an increasingly important consideration for businesses developing and deploying AI. “The global race is already creating growing competition for critical resources, from electricity supply and advanced chips to computing equipment, land and investment capital,” Lanzman added.

artigo.texto: Israel caps new data centers at 200 megawatts as demand overwhelms power grid The Electricity Authority will allocate an additional 1,000 megawatts to large data centers, bringing approved and planned capacity to about 3,000 megawatts. That would equal roughly 20% of projected national electricity consumption in 2030. After lengthy deliberations, the Electricity Authority published the main points of its new rules for connecting large data centers to Israel’s electricity grid on Sunday evening. As previously reported by Calcalist, the rules will cap the capacity of a new data center at 200 megawatts. The Authority will allocate an additional 1,000 megawatts to large data centers. Combined with approximately 2,000 megawatts in connections already approved, this would bring the total to around 3,000 megawatts, equivalent to about 20% of Israel’s projected electricity consumption in 2030. According to the Authority, the policy will make Israel “one of the world’s leaders in the rate of server farms relative to consumption.” The new rules became necessary after Noga, the company responsible for managing Israel’s electricity system, received requests to connect data centers with a combined capacity of 27,000 megawatts, roughly three times the country’s current average electricity consumption. In response to the surge in demand, the Electricity Authority issued a temporary order freezing responses to data center connection requests. To prevent developers from reserving grid capacity through projects with little chance of being built, or trading in connection approvals, the Authority will require developers to provide guarantees of NIS 2 million per megawatt of requested connection capacity, alongside additional conditions. The rules will also require backup mechanisms that allow data centers to be disconnected from the grid during periods of extreme demand. A 200-megawatt data center consumes electricity on a scale comparable to that of a mid-sized Israeli city, and construction costs are estimated at more than NIS 4 billion. The full decision is expected to be published in the coming days for a three-week public consultation. The Authority will consider the comments received and may make changes before the rules take effect. The decision would allow electricity consumption to grow as Israel attracts more data center investment, but it comes amid warnings that natural gas prices, and consequently electricity prices, could rise. A deal to supply natural gas involving NewMed and Ratio, partners in the Leviathan reservoir, collapsed. Last June, Israel Electric Corporation legal adviser Gershon Berkovitz warned that gas prices could increase. He also raised concerns about competition in the domestic market, warning that the problems could reach “the point of failure to meet the state’s energy needs.” While the new rules will restrict access to the grid for additional data centers and prevent the construction of some proposed megaprojects, including facilities with capacities of 500 megawatts and even 1,100 megawatts for which requests have already been submitted to Noga, limiting new connections will not eliminate the need for more electricity. Israel will still need to expand its generation capacity to meet growing demand from data centers and the wider economy.

artigo.texto: Award-winning technologies focus on LFP manufacturing efficiency, lithium-metal electrodes and battery performance prediction South Korean battery manufacturer SK On is accelerating research into cost-efficient lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries and next-generation lithium-metal technologies as it seeks to strengthen its competitiveness in the global battery market. The company announced on October 18 that it held its second Future Technology Institute Research Conference on October 14–15 at its R&D center in Daejeon, South Korea. Under the theme "Creating Our Future," the event brought together SK On President Lee Yong-wook, Future Technology Institute head Park Ki-soo and company researchers to share technological achievements and explore opportunities for collaboration. More than 300 research projects were submitted across six areas, including battery manufacturing processes, cells, systems, materials, next-generation technologies and platforms. The number of submissions increased approximately 15% from the previous year. LFP Manufacturing Innovation Takes Top Research Award The conference's grand prize went to a research team that developed a manufacturing process capable of replacing costly carbon nanotube (CNT) paste with CNT powder in LFP battery cathode production. CNTs are conductive materials that facilitate electron movement within battery electrodes. The research team developed a method to distribute CNT powder evenly throughout cathode materials, achieving performance comparable to conventional paste-based processes while improving cost competitiveness. SK On plans to evaluate the technology for potential application in commercial battery manufacturing. The development is particularly relevant as battery manufacturers seek to improve the economics of LFP batteries, which are increasingly used in electric vehicles and energy storage systems. Other award-winning projects included the design of large-format pouch-type lithium-metal battery electrodes and a predictive model for battery capacity degradation and internal resistance under different charging, discharging and storage conditions. The research projects were evaluated through a blind review process based on relevance, differentiation, contribution, originality and practical applicability. Digital Twin Technology Supports Next-Generation Battery Research The conference also featured a technology exhibition where researchers presented their projects, exchanged technical insights and participated in on-site evaluations. In a keynote presentation, Professor Lee Yong-min of Yonsei University discussed the current state and future prospects of digital twin technology in battery development. Digital twins create virtual representations of physical battery systems, enabling researchers to analyze performance and operating conditions through simulation. The technology could help improve development efficiency and support more accurate performance predictions. SK On plans to make the research conference a regular event to encourage knowledge sharing, strengthen collaboration and connect research achievements with practical product and manufacturing technologies. "The Future Technology Institute Research Conference is an important platform where our employees' challenges and research achievements contribute directly to SK On's technological competitiveness," said Lee Yong-wook, President of SK On. "We will continue to foster a research-driven culture and pursue technological innovation to lead the next-generation battery market," he added. The company aims to build on these research initiatives to strengthen its technology portfolio and manufacturing capabilities as competition intensifies across the global battery industry.

artigo.texto: Desvendando o potencial dos créditos de carbono florestal. (Baoquangngai.vn) - Com aproximadamente 826.000 hectares de floresta, Quang Ngai possui um potencial significativo para o desenvolvimento de créditos de carbono. A província está finalizando a coleta de dados, implementando projetos-piloto e explorando gradualmente o valor econômico das florestas, criando recursos adicionais para a proteção e o desenvolvimento florestal. Quang Ngai possui atualmente cerca de 826.000 hectares de floresta, incluindo aproximadamente 604.000 hectares de floresta natural e cerca de 222.000 hectares de floresta plantada. Com sua vasta área e diversidade de tipos e condições florestais, a província tem muitas oportunidades para pesquisar e implementar atividades que visem reduzir as emissões de gases de efeito estufa e desenvolver créditos de carbono florestal. Segundo o Instituto de Ciências Florestais do Vietnã, o potencial de carbono florestal de Quang Ngai pode ser explorado por meio de diversas soluções, tais como: proteção de florestas naturais, limitação do desmatamento e da degradação florestal, restauração e enriquecimento de florestas degradadas, melhoria da qualidade de florestas plantadas, conversão de pequenas florestas madeireiras em grandes florestas madeireiras, extensão do ciclo de negócios de florestas plantadas, manejo florestal sustentável, desenvolvimento de árvores dispersas e modelos agroflorestais. Essas atividades contribuem para a melhoria da qualidade florestal, a redução das emissões ou o aumento da capacidade de sequestro e armazenamento de carbono. Segundo o Sr. Nguyen Van Nam, chefe do Departamento Provincial de Proteção Florestal, com base em cálculos orientados pelo Departamento de Silvicultura e Proteção Florestal, as florestas da província absorvem e armazenam aproximadamente 2 milhões de toneladas de carbono anualmente, o equivalente a cerca de 2 milhões de créditos. Atualmente, a província está implementando o Programa de Redução de Emissões para as regiões Centro-Sul e Planalto Central, no âmbito da iniciativa LEAF, que deverá receber aproximadamente 1,13 milhão de créditos de carbono. Esses dados indicam que a província possui um potencial significativo para o desenvolvimento de créditos de carbono florestal. No entanto, a quantidade estimada de carbono absorvida e armazenada pelas florestas não corresponde necessariamente ao número de créditos que foram reconhecidos e são elegíveis para negociação. Para gerar valor econômico , os programas e projetos devem atender aos requisitos estipulados em relação aos métodos de cálculo, normas aplicáveis, medição, avaliação e verificação de resultados. A província de Quang Ngai está pesquisando o desenvolvimento de carbono florestal com o objetivo de reduzir as emissões de gases de efeito estufa e desenvolver projetos-piloto. Isso inclui o manejo e a proteção florestal sustentável, a prevenção de incêndios florestais e o manejo adequado da vegetação durante o reflorestamento, contribuindo para limitar os riscos de emissão, proteger os recursos florestais e fornecer uma base para avaliar os resultados da redução de emissões e considerar o acesso ao apoio de organizações não governamentais e empresas internacionais. Você também pode gostar Além disso, a província está coordenando o desenvolvimento de projetos-piloto de carbono florestal de acordo com padrões nacionais ou internacionais, com foco em florestas naturais e plantadas. Os resultados dos projetos devem ser avaliados, analisados, verificados e submetidos à autoridade competente para consideração e reconhecimento antes de participarem de transações no mercado de carbono, conforme regulamentado. Essas duas abordagens vinculam a proteção florestal ao objetivo de reduzir as emissões e gerar recursos financeiros adicionais. No entanto, para traduzir o potencial em valor tangível, é necessário demonstrar os resultados da redução de emissões, da manutenção da qualidade florestal e da conformidade com os padrões de cada programa e projeto. Criação de uma plataforma para o desenvolvimento de créditos de carbono florestal. Os dados sobre a área, o estado e as características de cada tipo de floresta são a base para determinar os estoques de carbono, monitorar as mudanças nos recursos e avaliar os resultados da implementação do projeto. Portanto, a coleta completa de dados florestais é uma das tarefas importantes para Quang Ngai, a fim de criar as condições necessárias para o desenvolvimento de créditos de carbono. O Departamento de Agricultura e Meio Ambiente está atualmente realizando um levantamento e inventário florestal, conforme orientação do Ministério da Agricultura e Meio Ambiente e do Comitê Popular Provincial. Isso também serve como base para o desenvolvimento e avaliação da viabilidade de projetos de carbono florestal. Essas áreas foram selecionadas com base no tamanho da área florestal, na extensão da floresta e na diversidade de tipos e condições florestais. artigo.texto: SK On announced on the 18th that it held the "2nd Future Technology Institute Academic Conference" at its Future Technology Institute in Yuseong-gu, Daejeon Metropolitan City, from the 14th to the 15th. The academic conference was conducted under the theme of "The Future We Create." Research projects were submitted across six fields: battery process, cell, system, materials, next-generation, and platform. The number of submissions was approximately 300, an increase of about 15% compared to last year. The grand prize went to Yeon Gu-tim-i (수상), who developed a process capable of replacing the expensive CNT paste used in the manufacturing of cathodes for LFP (lithium iron phosphate) batteries with CNT powder. CNT is a material utilized as a conductive agent that facilitates electron movement within battery electrodes. The company plans to consider applying this technology to actual production processes in the future. In addition, research teams that developed an electrode design for large-area pouch-type lithium metal batteries and a model predicting capacity degradation and internal resistance based on battery charge-discharge cycles and storage conditions received Choi U (수상) and the excellence award, respectively. The review was conducted in a blind format based on criteria such as topic relevance, research distinctiveness, contribution to outcomes, paper creativity, and practicality. SK On also held a technology exhibition centered on key research projects. Members explained their research content and engaged in question-and-answer sessions, while the technologies were evaluated through on-site voting. Lee Yong-wook, President of SK On, stated, "The Future Technology Institute Academic Conference, held for the second time following last year's event, is an important venue where members' challenges and research outcomes translate into SK On's technological competitiveness." He added, "We will further spread a research-centric culture and continue to drive technological innovation that leads the next-generation battery market."

artigo.texto: San Antonio is considering stricter regulations on data center development to address concerns about electricity use, water consumption, air quality, and neighborhood impact, with proposals requiring varying levels of City Council approval and community engagement. Public hearings are scheduled in October to decide on potential changes to the approval process for new data centers. - Data centers require significant electricity, cooling, and backup power, raising concerns amid rapid expansion in San Antonio. - Three regulatory proposals range from permitting data centers with specific requirements to requiring individual City Council approval and additional safeguards. - Mayor Gina Ortiz Jones proposes a 1,000-foot setback, advance community notice, neighborhood meetings, and green space replacement. - Council members are divided between ensuring resident input and maintaining economic development incentives. - Public hearings by the Zoning Commission and City Council are scheduled for October 20 and 29, respectively, allowing resident participation. San Antonio Moves Toward Tougher Data Center Restrictions as Residents Raise Concerns Over Water, Power and Neighborhoods San Antonio is moving closer to imposing stricter regulations on data centers as city leaders debate how to balance economic development with growing concerns about electricity consumption, water use, air quality and the impact of large industrial facilities on surrounding neighborhoods. The debate could change how data centers are approved throughout the city, potentially requiring developers to obtain City Council authorization before constructing new facilities. A public hearing before the Zoning Commission is scheduled for October 20, followed by an anticipated City Council vote October 29. Growing Industry Brings Growing Concerns Data centers house computer servers and other equipment supporting cloud computing, artificial intelligence and digital services. Their operations can require substantial electricity, cooling infrastructure and backup power systems. San Antonio has become an attractive market for developers because of available land, energy infrastructure and access to natural resources. However, the rapid expansion has raised questions about whether existing zoning regulations adequately protect residents. District 6 Councilman Ric Galvan has been among those pushing for stronger oversight, particularly as data center development expands across the city’s West Side. Galvan introduced a council consideration request last year calling for a comprehensive review of the industry’s impact on infrastructure and natural resources. “The residents of San Antonio deserve to have a say in where and how data centers are built in our city,” Galvan said in an October 15 statement. Three Proposals Could Reshape Development City officials are considering three approaches to regulating future facilities. One proposal would permit data centers in designated commercial and industrial districts if developers meet specific requirements, without requiring individual City Council approval. A second proposal would require developers to obtain specific use authorization, allowing council members to evaluate each project and providing opportunities for public comment. Mayor Gina Ortiz Jones has introduced a third approach combining individual council approval with additional safeguards. Her proposal includes a 1,000-foot setback, advance notice to affected communities, neighborhood engagement meetings and requirements to replace twice the green space eliminated during construction. The proposals also address concerns involving noise, lighting, emergency planning and environmental protections. Economic Growth Versus Neighborhood Protections Council members remain divided over how far the restrictions should go. Some argue that requiring individual approval for every facility would provide accountability and give residents a meaningful voice in decisions affecting their neighborhoods. Others warn that overly restrictive requirements could discourage investment and limit opportunities for economic development. Data centers could also generate additional revenue for municipally owned CPS Energy, potentially increasing funds transferred to the city. The central question is whether those economic benefits outweigh the demands placed on public infrastructure and surrounding communities. Residents Have Opportunity to Weigh In The Zoning Commission will consider the proposals October 20, with City Council expected to take up the issue October 29. Both meetings will provide opportunities for public participation. The outcome could determine whether data centers continue receiving approval under established zoning rules or face greater scrutiny from elected officials and residents. For communities already experiencing rapid development, the decision may establish how much influence neighborhoods have over the industry’s future expansion.

artigo.texto: How Long Was The First Samsung Galaxy Phone's Battery Life? The Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra offers about 16 hours of battery life on average, with some users reporting more than a day's worth of use. That's a solid battery life, but it took a lot of advancements and ingenuity to get here. To see how far battery technology has come, look back at the first device to bear the Galaxy name. Launched in 2009, the Samsung Galaxy I7500 was the first ever series release. It came with a 1,500 mAh removable battery and a quoted talk time of 9 hours and 20 minutes over a 2G connection, and 6 hours and 10 minutes over 3G. CNET reported it would barely last a day without recharging. Compared to the S26 Ultra's stats, of up to 52 hours of continuous talk time on a single charge, 6 to 9 hours doesn't seem like much. Yet, against some of the year's most popular phones, the Galaxy I7500 was about average. iPhone 3GS offered 5 hours of talk time via 3G, 12 hours via 2G. Meanwhile, the Samsung Eternity, another popular Samsung model, delivered up to 5 hours of talk time — though CNET stretched that further in testing — and the Nokia E52 could get up to 8 hours of talk time. However, even in 2009, devices weren't quite as feature-rich as what you might get today. Apple's iPhone and Samsung's earliest Galaxy models were a big step toward the modern smartphones we have now, crammed with extra hardware and functionality. Though it covers only 2013 to 2016, PhoneArena's study of battery improvements also shows how far we've come. The Samsung S and Note lines saw several battery upgrades in those years. Charging times improved significantly, too It's easy to get caught up in capacity improvements, which are, admittedly, a core part of any device's battery life. The bigger the battery, the longer it lasts, for the most part. However, another aspect of today's phone batteries makes a huge difference for convenience and performance: charging times. If your phone has a huge battery but takes forever to charge, that'll slow you down quite a bit throughout the day. You'll need to plug it in and wait for it to replenish, maybe for an inordinate amount of time. Of course, fast charging and high-power ports have changed that big time in something like the Galaxy S26 Ultra, which can charge to full in under an hour despite its 5,000 mAh battery. Many additional phones today have batteries the same size or larger. The original Galaxy, the I7500, would take about 2 to 3 hours to charge. That's nearly double what the S26 Ultra takes, but more importantly, its battery is less than half the size. Phones today can charge much larger batteries much faster. The PhoneArena battery study also shows battery charging times improving significantly between 2013 and 2016, decreasing exponentially. Fast forward to today, the Galaxy S26 also supports faster wireless charging, so you no longer need a cable for a quick battery boost. That was absolutely unheard of in 2009. Look at us go.

artigo.texto: HPQ Silicon has announced a new agreement with Aptera Motors Corp. to evaluate its HPQ ENDURA+ lithium-ion battery cells, marking a further step towards potential electric vehicle applications. The technology company confirmed that, alongside French technology partner Novacium SAS, it has signed a Cell Evaluation and Confidentiality Agreement with Aptera (NASDAQ: SEV), a US company developing solar-powered mobility solutions. Under the agreement, Aptera will carry out laboratory testing of HPQ ENDURA+ high-capacity 21700 lithium-ion cells. These cells use Novacium’s silicon-based anode materials and associated battery technology. HPQ ENDURA+ moves towards EV applications Aptera is developing a solar electric vehicle focused on aerodynamic efficiency, reduced energy consumption and integrated solar power generation. The company has reported receiving an EPA Certificate of Conformity for its 2026 Launch Edition and entering a manufacturing partnership with Launch Design. The evaluation will allow HPQ ENDURA+ cells to be assessed in an electric vehicle-related application where energy density and overall system efficiency are important considerations. HPQ Silicon president and chief executive Bernard Tourillon said the agreement reflects the company’s progress in moving from advanced materials development to high-performance battery cells and real-world application evaluation. Silicon-based battery technology under assessment Novacium has been developing silicon-based anode materials and related technologies intended to improve the energy-storage capabilities of conventional lithium-ion battery formats. HPQ holds relevant commercial rights to Novacium’s technology in North America and is involved in the commercial and industrial follow-up of potential future applications. Novacium chief operating officer Jed Kraiem said the evaluation would provide valuable application-level feedback on the company’s high-capacity cells. Novacium will support Aptera’s technical team throughout the testing process. Next steps for battery commercialisation The agreement supports HPQ Silicon’s strategy to establish a North American commercialisation pathway for HPQ ENDURA+, progressing from development and internal validation to external evaluation. However, the initial testing agreement does not represent a commitment to supply batteries commercially. Any further technical work, qualification or commercial arrangements will depend on the evaluation results and subsequent discussions between the parties. Image credit: HPQ.

artigo.texto: Funding Strains, Power Shortages and Local Opposition Hit Projects, Squeezing Chip Demand At Least 47 Large Data Center Projects in the United States In the United States, the world’s largest artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure market, at least 47 large-scale data center projects have faced disruptions this year alone. Concerns are rising that cracks are forming in the U.S. AI infrastructure boom, estimated to be worth $10 trillion, due to a combination of practical issues such as worsening corporate financial conditions, power shortages, and opposition from local residents. On Oct. 18 (local time), the Financial Times (FT) cited data from regulatory intelligence firm RegLayer, reporting that at least 47 data center development projects in the U.S. have been delayed, withdrawn, or halted this year. RegLayer explained, “We surveyed primarily large-scale worksites, and the figures were compiled conservatively.” Recently, investment bank (IB) Bernstein also estimated that only 35% of the data center construction projects currently planned in the U.S. are feasible. Funding shortages are cited as the primary cause of the successive disruptions in AI infrastructure projects in the U.S. Concerns have grown over the structure in which new operators take out loans to bear massive costs for purchasing GPUs and securing sites. In particular, the controversy intensified recently as the corporate bond yield of AI infrastructure company CoreWeave surged to the 15% level. CoreWeave is a so-called ‘neocloud’ company that operates a business of buying Nvidia AI chips to build data centers and then leasing the infrastructure to tech companies. The FT stated, “The overheating of infrastructure competition among companies has turned the overall AI industry into a ‘Wild West’,” adding, “Interest rate hikes and the bond market slump are threatening the ambitions of AI infrastructure companies.” The increasingly severe power shortage and opposition from local residents, who have begun to perceive data centers as undesirable facilities, are also stumbling blocks. Big tech company Oracle notified the developer of the 2.45GW (gigawatt) ‘Project Jupiter’ underway in New Mexico of force majeure last month in preparation for disruptions in securing power. The intent is to delay rent payments if the set schedule is not met. PJM, the largest power grid operator in the US, recently decided to halt a previously planned special auction for 15 years’ worth of power for data centers to respond to the AI-driven power shortage. According to the FT’s own survey results, it was found that more than 1,000 communities in the US have attempted to introduce temporary halts or restrictive measures related to AI infrastructure development this year. Concerns over AI infrastructure companies are emerging in various parts of the market beyond the US. It is reported that Nscale, a British neocloud company, is also pursuing an initial public offering (IPO) with a corporate value of about $30 billion, but is facing difficulties as investors’ expectations are much lower than this. Bloomberg reported that due to the recently deteriorated industry conditions, some investors view Nscale’s corporate value at $16 billion to $19 billion. Previously, Australian AI infrastructure company Firmus also withdrew its IPO plan, which had been pursued at a scale of about $5 billion. It is pointed out that such crises for AI infrastructure companies could ultimately affect the earnings of semiconductor manufacturers. This is because if infrastructure companies increasingly struggle to secure investment funds and construction plans are consequently delayed, they may delay or reduce orders for semiconductor chips to be used in data centers. In fact, the stock prices of domestic memory companies such as Samsung Electronics and SK hynix have continued to show weakness recently. This is due to worsened investor sentiment caused by concerns over U.S. interest rate hikes and the pace adjustment of AI infrastructure. Bloomberg stated, “As borrowing costs rise and uncertainty about the long-term profitability of AI technology grows, investor sentiment regarding overall AI infrastructure, including server companies and semiconductor manufacturers, has deteriorated.”

artigo.texto: Two-Year LTA Covers 2027 Supply of High-Voltage Switchgear LS Electric has accelerated its push into the North American data center market after winning power infrastructure supply rights worth 170.0 billion won ($125.80 million) from a major U.S. tech company. LS Electric said on Oct. 19 that it signed a contract to supply power distribution solutions for data centers in North America. The agreement was structured as a long-term agreement, or LTA, running for two years from 2027 to 2028. The order value of 170.0 billion won ($125.80 million) corresponds to the volume scheduled for supply in 2027, while the scale of the 2028 business is to be finalized through additional consultations later. The main product to be supplied is 38kV-class high-voltage switchgear. The equipment serves as core infrastructure that stably distributes high-voltage electricity entering data centers and protects facilities when abnormalities occur in the power system. Given the nature of artificial intelligence, or AI, data centers, which must continuously receive large-scale electricity around the clock, product reliability and quality acted as key indicators in the contract. LS Electric is seeking to expand beyond this high-voltage switchgear supply. It is understood to be holding additional discussions on supplying other customized high-end power equipment for data centers, including low-voltage switchgear, distribution transformers, and ring main units, or RMUs. The latest result is seen as reflecting the effectiveness of the company’s strategy of strengthening its local response system in the United States. LS Electric has established bases at LS Electric Utah in Cedar City, Utah, and the Bastrop Campus in Texas. Through these operations, it has built a locally completed value chain that handles the full process on site, from sales and design to production, commissioning, and service, enabling it to respond quickly to customer demands. An LS Electric official explained that trust built through world-class technological capabilities and project execution experience led to the long-term contract. The company said it plans to further strengthen a stable revenue base and improve profitability by increasing supplies of high-value-added products for data centers in the future.

artigo.texto: AI Data Centers Snap Up Optical Fiber, Spot Prices Soar 5x Year-on-Year, Shortage Could Persist Through 2028 The AI data center (AIDC) construction boom is pushing optical fiber from a supporting role into the spotlight. TrendForce's latest communications industry research estimates that the global optical fiber supply-demand gap will reach 180 million fiber-kilometers in 2026. The supply crunch is directly reflected in pricing, with spot prices for finished optical fiber up 2.8 to more than 5 times compared with 2025, and the tight conditions are expected to last at least through 2028. The research notes that global optical fiber supply began tightening at the end of 2025, driven primarily by the massive new demand created by AI data center-related applications. There is no slack left on the supply side: global optical fiber capacity utilization is projected to rise to 92% in 2026, inventory levels have been compressed from four months in 2024 to just one month, and some major manufacturers' order books are already filled through the first quarter of 2027 — meaning existing capacity is running near full. Expanding capacity is not something that happens overnight. Optical fiber preform expansion involves the installation of deposition equipment and process setup, requiring roughly 18 to 24 months from planning to production. Even if manufacturers launch expansion plans now, new supply will take time to come online, making it difficult to effectively ease the shortage in the near term. Demand remains robust. The research estimates global optical fiber demand at 577 million fiber-kilometers in 2026, with growth driven mainly by data center construction, which accounts for roughly 18% to 20% of total demand and is expected to rise further to 30% to 35% in 2027. In addition to large Cloud Service Providers continuing to expand AI data centers, chipmakers and telecom operators are also investing in related infrastructure, driving optical fiber consumption for data center interconnect and high-capacity backbone networks. The supply-demand imbalance is already reflected in spot quotes across optical fiber product categories. Broken down by application, bend-insensitive fiber used for cabling inside data centers has seen the steepest increase, with average prices in 2026 more than 5x higher than in 2025. AI backbone fiber used for data center interconnect and high-capacity backbone networks has risen about 2.8x year-on-year. Mainstream fiber for telecom services has also climbed about 3.7x. Note: Year-on-year increases reflect the change in 2026 average prices versus 2025 average prices. Faced with persistently tightening supply, telecom operators' procurement strategies have clearly shifted. The previous model centered on short-term purchasing is gradually giving way to long-term contracts that lock in resources in advance. For example, Verizon and Corning signed a multi-year supply agreement in September 2026, planning to secure more than 129 million fiber-kilometers (about 80 million miles) of high-density optical fiber and connectivity solutions between 2027 and 2032. In addition to supporting broadband buildouts, the fiber will be used for high-capacity backbone networks connecting AI data centers. The nature of this tightness differs from past telecom buildout cycles. The research argues that the root of this shortage is the continuous expansion of new AI data center-related demand, rather than a cyclical rebound in traditional telecom capital spending. With supply unable to ramp up quickly in the short term and demand growing steadily, it will become increasingly common for telecom operators and large infrastructure players to lock in optical fiber resources through long-term contracts in advance. For the industry chain, optical fiber's shift from a buyer's market to a seller's market means upstream preform and fiber manufacturers have significantly strengthened their pricing power, along with extended order visibility. Conversely, telecom carriers and data center operators face rising construction costs, making procurement timing and cost control increasingly important. The market's focus has shifted from "is there demand" to "can we get the material" — and the pace at which optical fiber supply chain capacity comes online will be a key indicator for tracking AI infrastructure progress over the next two years.

artigo.texto: SK On Develops CNT Powder Process to Cut LFP Costs, Wins Top Prize at Future Technology Institute Conference SK On has developed a new process that can lower the manufacturing cost of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cathodes. The technology replaces the expensive carbon nanotube (CNT) paste previously used with a powder form while maintaining equivalent performance, and the company plans to review its applicability to actual mass production processes. The research achievement was selected as the grand prize winner at the "2nd Future Technology Institute Academic Conference" held over two days starting October 14 at the Future Technology Institute in Yuseong-gu, Daejeon. This year's event was held under the theme "The Future We Create," with SK On President Lee Yong-wook and Future Technology Institute Director Park Ki-soo in attendance. A total of approximately 300 research projects were submitted across six categories: battery process, cell, system, materials, next-generation technology, and platform. This represents an increase of about 15% compared to last year. Award winners were selected through a blind review process based on five criteria: topic relevance, research differentiation, contribution to outcomes, creativity, and practicality. The grand prize-winning research team secured technology to uniformly disperse CNT powder into cathode materials. CNT serves as a conductive agent that facilitates electron movement within battery electrodes. The use of powder form was highly evaluated for its potential to replace the relatively expensive paste process and reduce manufacturing costs. SK On plans to review whether the technology can be applied to actual production processes. The top excellence award went to a research team that developed electrode design technology for large-area pouch-type lithium-metal batteries. The excellence award was given to a team that developed a model predicting capacity degradation and internal resistance based on repeated battery charge-discharge cycles and storage conditions. The conference also featured a technology exhibition showcasing key research achievements. Researchers directly explained their technologies and conducted Q&A sessions, with the exhibition operated through on-site voting by members to evaluate the technologies. The keynote speech was delivered by Professor Lee Yong-min of Yonsei University. He introduced the current status and outlook of digital twin technology, which implements actual battery designs in virtual space to analyze performance and condition. In the subsequent Q&A session, he exchanged views on battery technology with SK On members and discussed the latest trends in industry-academia collaboration. Strengthening LFP Battery Price Competitiveness SK On's process development aligns with the growing importance of LFP battery price competitiveness in the global battery market. While LFP batteries have lower energy density than nickel-cobalt-manganese (NCM) batteries, they are cheaper to produce and offer higher thermal stability, driving rapid demand growth alongside the expansion of electric vehicle adoption. With Chinese battery manufacturers leading the LFP market, South Korean companies are also making all-out efforts to secure cost-reduction technologies. The process of replacing CNT paste with powder carries significant meaning in this price competition. Paste form offers the advantage of easy dispersion but contains solvents, making it more expensive with higher storage and transportation costs. Converting to powder form can simultaneously reduce material and logistics costs while maintaining the same performance. However, the technical difficulty of uniformly dispersing powder is high, making it a key question whether the research team's achievement can translate into actual mass production. The top excellence award for lithium-metal battery electrode design technology is also noteworthy. Lithium-metal batteries are considered a next-generation technology that can significantly increase energy density by replacing the graphite anode of conventional lithium-ion batteries with lithium metal. Electrode design for large-area pouch-type cells is one of the key challenges for commercialization. Institutionalizing as a Platform for Sharing Research Achievements SK On plans to make the academic conference a regular event to expand technical exchange and collaboration among researchers. The company views a systematic structure for sharing and evaluating internal research achievements as a foundation for enhancing next-generation battery technology competitiveness. President Lee Yong-wook said, "The Future Technology Institute Academic Conference, now in its second year, is an important venue where our members' challenges and research achievements translate into SK On's technology competitiveness. We will further spread a research-centric culture and continue technological innovation to lead the next-generation battery market." SK On currently operates production bases in the U.S. states of Georgia and Kentucky, as well as Hungary and China, while simultaneously preparing for LFP battery mass production and developing next-generation technologies such as lithium-metal and solid-state batteries. How quickly the research achievements from this conference can be applied to actual products and processes will serve as a test of the company's future technology competitiveness.
