artigo.texto: Shinhan Asset Management's SOL All-Solid-State Battery ETF Ranks No. 1 Among South Korean Equity ETFs With 22.76% Three-Month Return Shinhan Asset Management's "SOL All-Solid-State Battery & Silicon Anode" exchange-traded fund (ETF) has posted the highest return among South Korean-listed equity ETFs over the past three months. As of the 16th of this month, the product's three-month return stood at 22.76%, ranking first among South Korean-listed equity ETFs excluding leveraged and inverse products. That is 39.66 percentage points ahead of the KOSPI's -16.90% over the same period. The ETF concentrates investments in key companies tied to all-solid-state batteries and silicon anodes. All-solid-state batteries replace conventional liquid electrolytes with solid materials to boost safety and energy density, and expectations for their commercialization have recently been rising. Major holdings include Samsung SDI, which is pursuing mass production of all-solid-state batteries; LG Energy Solution, a key energy storage system (ESS) player; EcoPro BM, an all-solid-state cathode materials company; ISU Specialty Chemical, a lithium sulfide-related company; battery materials company Lotte Energy Materials; and silicon anode company Daejoo Electronic Materials. The portfolio is built around next-generation battery technology advancement and industrial structural change rather than short-term shifts in electric vehicle demand. The secondary battery sector has recently been shaking off a prolonged correction driven by slowing electric vehicle demand and securing new growth drivers. Rising ESS demand from the spread of artificial intelligence (AI) data centers is translating into improved earnings at battery companies, and investment sentiment is recovering as expectations build for commercialization of next-generation technologies such as all-solid-state batteries and silicon anodes. The fact that secondary battery-related ETFs have ranked among the top performers while the South Korean semiconductor sector's rally has stalled is seen in the same light. ESS is emerging as a key growth driver reshaping a secondary battery industry that had been centered on electric vehicles. As power demand from AI data centers grows and renewable energy generation expands, the importance of stable power supply and energy storage has increased. LG Energy Solution posted preliminary third-quarter operating profit of 756 billion won (approximately $566.2 million), topping market expectations. The company's earnings recovery is attributed to expansion of its North American ESS business and conversion of production facilities. The fact that commercialization timelines for next-generation batteries are taking concrete shape is also working in favor of investment sentiment. Samsung SDI is pursuing technology development and cooperation with customers with the goal of mass-producing all-solid-state batteries in 2027. South Korean materials companies are also moving to secure production capacity for key raw materials, and the South Korean government plans to support next-generation battery research and development worth about 400 billion won (approximately $299.6 million) over five years starting in 2027. All-solid-state batteries are expected to see their applications broaden beyond electric vehicles to humanoid robots and the aerospace sector. Kim Jung-hyun, head of Shinhan Asset Management's ETF business group, said, "The secondary battery industry is securing a new demand base through ESS, and growth drivers are diversifying as commercialization of next-generation technologies such as all-solid-state batteries and silicon anodes becomes visible." He added, "Going forward, earnings recovery through ESS and competitiveness in next-generation technologies such as all-solid-state batteries will be key factors determining corporate value."

artigo.texto: South Korea's LS Electric Signs approximately $125 Million AI Data Center Power Distribution Deal with U.S. Big Tech South Korea's LS Electric (010120) has signed a long-term supply agreement (LTA) worth approximately 169 billion won (approximately $126.8 million) with a U.S. Big Tech company for power distribution solutions for artificial intelligence (AI) data centers. As AI infrastructure expansion drives a clear shift in power equipment procurement from short-term orders to long-term volume commitments, analysts say the company has secured a bridgehead to broaden its supply range from high-voltage switchgear to high-end product lines. LS Electric said in a regulatory filing on the 19th that it had signed a $125.23 million (~169 billion won) contract to supply power distribution solutions for North American data centers. The contract runs for two years from 2027 to 2028, and the order value corresponds to volumes scheduled for delivery in 2027. The 2028 supply volume will be finalized through additional negotiations with the company. The main supply item is 38kV-class high-voltage switchgear. This equipment distributes extra-high-voltage power coming from outside at appropriate levels to each computing facility inside the data center and cuts off circuits when abnormal currents such as leakage or short circuits occur, protecting critical servers. In AI data centers where large-scale computation runs around the clock, continuity of power quality and equipment reliability determine operational success, and analysts say demand for high-reliability distribution equipment is bound to grow structurally. Global Big Tech companies have recently favored long-term supply agreements to secure stable power solutions for AI data center construction. As data center construction demand grows rapidly, the view that power equipment supply contracts themselves will be reorganized around long-term deals is gaining traction. Some skeptics argue that returns on AI infrastructure investment may be short-lived, but large-scale data center expansion continues on the judgment that AI will become fundamental infrastructure going forward. Building on this contract, LS Electric is also negotiating additional supply of data center-tailored power equipment such as low-voltage switchgear, distribution-class transformers, and RMUs (high-voltage gas-insulated load break switches). The goal is to expand its supply scope from a single high-voltage switchgear item to data center power infrastructure overall. The company is also strengthening its local North American response system. Centered on LS Electric Utah in Cedar City, Utah, and the Bastrop Campus in Texas, it has built a value chain that completes sales, design, production, and service locally, supplying products tailored to each customer's needs. The strategy is seen as aimed at reducing tariff and logistics risks while improving delivery responsiveness. An LS Electric official said, "Our world-class data center solution technology and the trust built through executing customized projects led to this long-term supply agreement," adding, "We will continue to expand supply of high-value-added products for data centers to secure a stable revenue base and maximize profitability." The deal is significant in that it is a case of North American AI data center-driven demand for power equipment translating into long-term results for a South Korean manufacturer, and could lead to expanded exports of adjacent product groups such as transformers and circuit breakers. However, since the contract value is limited to the 2027 portion and 2028 volumes remain undetermined, actual revenue recognition is expected to depend on the outcome of further negotiations and data center construction schedules.

artigo.texto: Li Xiang on "making cars doesn't mean making batteries": Li Auto aims to be the automaker that understands batteries best On October 19, Li Xiang, chairman and CEO of Li Auto (02015.HK), posted on social media to lay out the industry value of automakers developing core battery technology in-house. He argued that ultra-large-scale industries need "two legs advancing alternately"—one being specialized suppliers with a deep understanding of the product, the other being OEMs that delve deeply into core technologies. "The world needs both battery companies that best understand smart electric vehicles and smart EV companies that best understand batteries," Li wrote. He did not name names directly, but the remarks were widely interpreted as a response to earlier comments by Ni Jun, chief manufacturing officer of CATL (300750.SZ). In mid-to-late September, asked about automakers developing their own batteries at CATL's "Global Quality Open Month" event, Ni said: "Making cars doesn't mean making batteries. You still need professionals to do professional things." He also noted that how far a car can go and how long it lasts "is not determined by the best cell, but by the worst one." This time Li did not maintain a confrontational stance. He stressed that partner battery suppliers remain partners, and that which steps to do in-house and which to do with partners are choices made at different stages, with only one criterion—which approach is better for users. He also said Li Auto will hold an electric technology launch event on October 20 to announce its latest technological progress. This was not the first time Li has spoken publicly about the in-house development route. On September 28, he published a long post responding to discussion about "de-CATL-ization," saying zero-sum thinking is not how Li Auto defines its in-house strategy, and describing CATL as Li Auto's "comrade-in-arms." "Self-developed and self-manufactured PACK, self-developed cells with contract manufacturing" Li Auto sums up its battery approach as "self-developed and self-manufactured PACK, self-developed cells with contract manufacturing": Li Auto leads cell design and R&D, production is contracted to battery makers such as Sunwoda (300207.SZ) and CALB (03931.HK), while the battery pack, BMS and thermal management are developed and manufactured in-house by Li Auto. Capital-level ties are already in place. On September 4, Sunwoda announced that Li Auto had injected 2.65 billion yuan (approximately $396.6 million) into Sunwoda Power for an 8.79% stake; Li Auto and its affiliates hold a combined ~11.17%, making it the second-largest shareholder of Sunwoda Power. Business registration information shows that Shandong Li Auto Battery Technology Co., Ltd. was recently registered in Xuecheng District, Zaozhuang City, Shandong Province, with registered capital of 10 million yuan (approximately $1.5 million), wholly owned by Beijing Li Auto Co., Ltd., with a business scope focused on battery components and energy recovery systems. In October 2025, Li Auto had also set up a joint venture with Sunwoda Power, Shandong Li Auto Battery Co., Ltd., with registered capital of 300 million yuan (approximately $44.9 million), each holding 50%. The pace of battery deployment is accelerating in tandem. The L8, L6 and i8 already use self-developed batteries; new-generation MEGA models ordered through the Li Auto app from September 7 switch to self-developed 5C ternary lithium batteries, with deliveries expected to begin in November; the i9 launched in mid-September still uses CATL 5C batteries in its first batch; and the 2026 i6 to be launched in the fourth quarter will carry both self-developed 5C batteries and Li Auto's self-developed Mach chip, with plans to no longer offer a CATL version. Note: The above deployment plans are compiled from public reports; specific configurations are subject to Li Auto's official announcements. System integration innovation becomes the focus of competition and cooperation On cooperation models, Li Auto takes an open approach. Li Auto President Ma Donghui said in an earlier interview that as sales grow and capacity demand rises, the company very much wants to work with leading battery makers, but the prerequisite is that underlying data must be connected. He noted that OEMs do not think only from the perspective of battery components, but instead consider the battery together with all electrical components, thermal management and control systems of the vehicle, designing collaboratively from the vehicle architecture. This points to a shift in the innovation path for power batteries: as OEMs become more deeply involved in battery R&D, the industry's innovation focus may move from the performance of a single component to system integration innovation between the battery and the vehicle. For battery companies, this means the competitive dimension extends from cell metrics to data interfaces, thermal management and vehicle integration capability; for automakers, a model of parallel in-house development and contract manufacturing allows them to hold core definition rights while avoiding heavy-asset investment. In his latest post, Li reiterated that walking on two legs is not one company's choice but the entire industry's, and the progress it drives ultimately benefits users. He also warned that if the industry relies on only one leg for a long time, hopping on one foot is hard to sustain over long distances, and companies can easily fall into scale competition while the performance, quality, safety and lifespan that users truly care about stall in place. Notably, the pace of Li Auto's in-house battery push is rising in step with its supply chain bargaining power. From injecting capital into Sunwoda Power to setting up a battery technology company, and now to the gradual switch of mainstream models to self-developed cells, Li Auto is turning batteries from a purchased part into a defining component. artigo.texto: BYD Exports '9-Minute Charging' Ecosystem to Indonesia, Putting Hyundai Motor and South Korean Batteries on the Back Foot in Southeast Asia China's BYD has moved into overseas markets by building an ultra-fast charging network in Indonesia that can charge an electric-vehicle battery in nine minutes. Under an "ecosystem export" model that bundles finished vehicles, batteries and charging infrastructure into a single package, the push is increasing pressure on Hyundai Motor and Kia, which trail China in both charging speed and infrastructure, as well as on South Korea's three major battery makers. BYD said on Oct. 19 that it unveiled plans on Oct. 14 in Jakarta to build a flash-charging network of up to 1,500 kW and simultaneously introduced the new D9 and Z9GT from Denza, its premium brand. The project marks the first time BYD's ultra-fast charging technology has been deployed outside China. According to the company, the flash chargers combine an energy storage system (ESS) and are the world's first to use a T-shaped suspended design that reduces the weight burden of the charging cable. They also feature plug-and-charge functionality, with authentication and payment completed simply by connecting the vehicle. BYD plans to install chargers first at 10 Denza showrooms to create customer touchpoints, then gradually expand to public charging networks starting at the end of the year. The network will be open to vehicles of all brands, but top speeds will be available only on cars equipped with compatible batteries. Charging performance reaches 70% from a 10% state of charge in five minutes and 97% in nine minutes. The second-generation Blade Battery underpinning this is a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery that BYD first unveiled in China in March, with energy density 5% higher than the first generation. Even at minus 30 degrees Celsius, it charges from 20% to 97% in 12 minutes. The Z9GT equipped with this battery claims a driving range of 1,036 kilometers. The new D9, a luxury multi-purpose vehicle (MPV), is the first model to apply both the second-generation Blade Battery and flash-charging technology. Indonesia is the testing ground for the packaged market entry BYD is pushing. Since entering the market in 2024, BYD has sold Chinese-made finished vehicles while receiving duty-free import benefits in exchange for committing to invest in a local plant. When the local production obligation began in 2026-2027, BYD completed a plant in Subang, West Java (annual capacity of up to 150,000 units) on the third of last month and halted finished-vehicle imports. It plans to sell down remaining inventory and then replace imports with locally produced vehicles. BYD and Denza are said to have captured 40% of Indonesia's local EV market within two years of entry. However, the pace of building overseas charging networks is slower than originally planned. In June, the company outlined a plan to build 3,000 stations in Europe by the end of this year, but at this month's Paris Motor Show the target was revised to 100 by year-end and 3,000 by the end of 2027 — effectively a one-year delay. The gap with South Korean competitors is evident in the numbers. Hyundai Motor's Ioniq 5 and Kia's EV6 take about 18 minutes to charge from 10% to 80% on 350 kW chargers — more than three times the speed BYD is touting, on a simple comparison. There is also a gap in exporting charging ecosystems. Hyundai Motor and Kia, through Ionna — a U.S. charging joint venture founded by eight automakers — expanded their U.S. charging sites from 90 at the start of this year to more than 200 by mid-October. Another 80 are under construction, with a goal of 30,000 fast chargers by 2030. But because Ionna is a consortium jointly funded by multiple companies, its structure differs from BYD-style vertical integration, in which a single company sells batteries, vehicles and chargers together. In Indonesia, Chinese capital continues to flow into battery value-chain investment. A consortium including affiliates of China's CATL has launched an integrated project worth about $6 billion (approximately 8 trillion won) spanning nickel mining through battery production and recycling. The LG Energy Solution consortium, by contrast, withdrew last year from an 11 trillion won (approximately $8.3 billion) battery value-chain project. The Indonesian government is bringing in new Chinese investors to carry the follow-up project forward. Chinese dominance is also clear in global market share. According to SNE Research, in terms of global EV battery usage from January to August this year, CATL held 39.4% and BYD 15.1%, with seven Chinese companies combined accounting for 73.3%. LG Energy Solution held third place at 8.1%, but that was down 1.5 percentage points from a year earlier. The market is watching the project as a variable that could reshape competition in Southeast Asia's EV market. artigo.texto: Chinese EV and Battery Makers Build 26 Plants in Europe, Sidestepping Tariffs for Duty-Free Market Grab Chinese EV and battery companies are rapidly expanding local production bases across Europe, effectively sidestepping tariff barriers. The number of Chinese-owned EV and battery plants either under construction or already operating in Europe has reached 26. Chinese companies have shifted away from the strategy of manufacturing cheaply at home and exporting, instead building factories directly in Europe to sell tariff-free. In Szeged, southern Hungary, BYD—China's top EV maker—is building a factory on a 3 million square meter site, roughly the size of Seoul's Yeouido district. Once completed by the end of this year, BYD will become the first Chinese passenger EV company to be fully exempt from the European Union's 27% tariff. CATL, the world's largest battery maker, has built its largest battery plant outside China in Debrecen, Hungary. The facility, backed by a €7.3 billion (approximately $8.2 billion) investment, has an annual production capacity of 100 gigawatt-hours (GWh). The first of three planned plants began operations earlier this month, with European automakers including Mercedes-Benz having placed advance orders covering several years of output. Jin Liang, CATL's Debrecen plant manager, said: "Given the lower skill levels of workers in Europe, we have set a higher automation rate than in China. We plan to re-export this system to China soon, as it represents our most advanced facilities to date." CATL chose European production to avoid EU tariff and regulatory uncertainty. Unlike the United States, the EU does not outright block Chinese battery makers from entering, but it is preparing to introduce the Industrial Acceleration Act (IAA), which provides incentives to companies producing within Europe. EVs must be assembled in the EU and source more than 70% of components—excluding batteries—from within the region to qualify for subsidies. "This will serve as a base that eliminates uncertainties such as future EU export restrictions or tariff hikes," he said. "CATL will make in Europe, work for Europe, and become a member of Europe." Europe's Battery Self-Sufficiency Ambitions Collapse The intensifying Chinese offensive comes against the backdrop of Europe's own battery industry collapse. Northvolt, once hailed as "Europe's battery hope," filed for bankruptcy in March last year after failing to withstand production disruptions and funding shortages. Its core assets—the Swedish plant and R&D facilities—were transferred to U.S. battery company Lyten in February this year. ACC, a battery joint venture co-invested by Stellantis, Mercedes-Benz, and TotalEnergies, has also scrapped plans to build plants in Germany and Italy. Europe's "battery self-sufficiency" vision has effectively crumbled. European automakers are also struggling with the EV transition. Volkswagen Group's operating margin fell to 3.8% in the first half of this year, its worst performance since COVID-19. The company has begun cutting approximately 100,000 jobs and reducing vehicle lineup and production capacity. Stellantis and Ford are handing over some of their European production facilities to Chinese companies. Kilian Csaba, president of the Hungarian Automobile Association, said: "After Europe's manufacturing industry, including automobiles, collapsed, Chinese companies are rapidly filling the void. This will pose a major threat to South Korean companies as well." Why Hungary Became the Chosen Hub CATL selected Hungary as its European base due to geographic advantages. Key materials and components can be sourced from Hungary, Poland, and other nearby countries, while proximity to automotive plants in Germany and elsewhere reduces logistics costs. The Debrecen region has a dense battery value chain, including South Korea's EcoPro BM cathode material plant and China's Semcorp separator plant. In northwestern Hungary, Solus Advanced Materials operates a battery copper foil plant and Soulbrain runs an electrolyte facility. Expanding the scope to nearby Poland, Belgium's Umicore also operates a cathode material plant. Kaderják Péter, president of the Hungarian Battery Industry Association, explained: "With environmental regulations tightening across Europe recently, obtaining permits for new battery plants has become more difficult. Companies that have already secured or are preparing facilities will hold a clear advantage." China's Accelerating Encroachment on the European Market The number of Chinese battery companies building or operating plants in Europe has reached 14. Gotion plans to establish plants totaling 50 GWh in Spain and Slovakia in partnership with Volkswagen. EVE Energy has begun operating a 28 GWh battery plant in Hungary. The total battery cell plant capacity Chinese companies plan to operate in Europe reaches 282.8 GWh—far exceeding the 160 GWh European production capacity of South Korea's three major battery makers. The European battery market landscape has shifted dramatically. In the January-August period this year, the top seven Chinese companies held a 67.8% share of the European market, surging 26.8 percentage points from 41.0% in 2023. Over the same period, South Korea's three major battery makers saw their share halve from 55.6% to 28.7%. Chinese companies are expanding not only production bases but also R&D and design centers across Europe. Geely Group has established centers in Frankfurt, Germany and Gothenburg, Sweden; BYD in Budapest, Hungary; and XPeng and Xiaomi in Munich, Germany—all vying for European talent. Note: Chinese companies are pursuing or operating a total of 26 EV and battery plants in Europe.

artigo.texto: Uncertain carbon credit revenues in agriculture are making it difficult to assess how much projects can earn beyond their core business activities. Nguyen Thi Thu Ha, deputy head of Agribank’s Steering Committee for Environmental, Social, and Governance, highlighted these constraints and more at VIR’s seminar on credit policy and the carbon market last week in Hanoi. She said financing arrangements needed to reflect project viability, repayment capacity, and the timing of expected returns. “Carbon credit revenue can supplement project returns, but it cannot be treated as a reliable source of repayment before the conditions for generating and selling those credits are established,” said Ha. Vietnam’s shift towards lower-emission production is creating funding needs beyond equipment and technology. Businesses must also pay for project preparation, environmental monitoring, and changes to production processes, while ensuring that investments generate sufficient returns to service debt. “The domestic carbon market remains at an early stage, making the commercial contribution of carbon credits dependent on project readiness and market development,” she added. Vietnam has continued to develop the regulatory framework for emissions reduction and carbon market activities, including plans for a domestic carbon exchange and rules governing international carbon credit transactions. Greenhouse gas inventory requirements have also expanded. The number of covered facilities rose from 1,912 in 2022 to 2,441 in September 2026. Criteria have also been expanded for identifying green projects, including circular economy activities. However, meeting environmental requirements does not in itself make a project commercially viable or eligible for bank financing. Businesses may still need feasibility studies, technical assessments, environmental monitoring systems, and agreements covering production, purchasing, and the distribution of financial benefits. In agriculture and rural development, low-emission rice cultivation, livestock waste treatment, sustainable forestry, and biomass utilisation require funding at different stages of the value chain. Financing must account for the needs of farmers, cooperatives, and processors, as well as seasonal production cycles, market access and operating costs. Across the value chain Green projects require funding at several stages, from feasibility studies and environmental assessments to equipment, working capital, monitoring, and compliance. For small producers, the cost of preparing a project can be a barrier before any return is generated. Once operations begin, maintenance and verification add to expenditure, while purchasing and processing businesses need capital to handle agricultural output. For that reason, Ha emphasised the need to align financing with project costs and cash flow cycles. In agriculture, adopting new cultivation methods can increase expenses before additional income materialises, while seasonal production and delays between delivery and payment can put pressure on borrowers’ liquidity. “Financing arrangements need to reflect the costs incurred at each stage of a project, the timing of expected cash flows and the borrower’s repayment capacity,” Ha said. Commercial loans can finance equipment and working capital where credible repayment sources exist, while technical assistance, concessional funding, and guarantees may help cover project preparation costs or address specific risks. The source of repayment is particularly important for projects that expect to earn carbon credit revenue. Reduced energy and material consumption can lower operating costs directly, but income from carbon credits depends on project eligibility, verification, buyer demand, and payment terms. “Businesses cannot treat carbon credit revenue in the same way as savings from reduced energy or material consumption. Income from credits depends on whether emissions reductions can be verified and the credits sold,” she added. Agribank’s existing agricultural lending provides a channel for financing investment in lower-emission production, according to Ha. By mid-2026, the bank’s assets exceeded $108 billion, deposits surpassed $100 billion and outstanding loans topped $80 billion. At the end of August, lending to agriculture, farmers, and rural areas exceeded $53.6 billion, equivalent to 64.7 per cent of total outstanding loans. She also outlined the bank’s reach among smaller borrowers. As of July 31, Agribank’s more than 58,000 lending groups comprised over 910,000 members, with total loans exceeding $8.64 billion. “These established lending relationships could provide a route to identifying farmers and cooperatives seeking to invest in resource efficiency or emissions reduction. However, such projects would still need to meet the bank’s lending requirements, including those relating to project readiness and repayment capacity,” Ha shared. Agribank’s green credit programmes provide further funding channels. Its green credit portfolio stood at nearly $1.2 billion at the end of March. For the year, the bank has allocated $120 million to a programme targeting individual customers and $2 billion to clean and high-tech agriculture. It also operates a programme worth at least $1.2 billion to support production, processing, and consumption under the Mekong Delta’s one-million-hectare project for high-quality, low-emission rice cultivation. The rice initiative illustrates the need to coordinate financing across the agricultural supply chain. Farmers may require seasonal loans to adopt new cultivation methods, while cooperatives need equipment and working capital to coordinate production and collect data. Technical partners can provide training and support environmental measurement, while processors need funds to purchase and handle the crop. “Financing needs to be considered across the value chain, from production and data collection to purchasing and processing,” Ha said. artigo.texto: Italy and five other member states have failed to secure a further postponement of the EU’s new carbon market for heating and transport fuels, although European leaders have ordered a fresh assessment of its impact on households and businesses. European Union leaders have resisted demands for another postponement of carbon pricing for road transport and building fuels, exposing deep disagreements over climate policy, industrial competitiveness and the burden of energy costs on European households. At the European Council summit in Brussels on 15–16 October, the Visegrad countries — Poland, Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic — pressed for the second European Emissions Trading System, known as ETS2, to be delayed until 2030. Italy and Greece joined calls for greater flexibility over carbon costs, although Rome also sought a national exemption from aspects of the energy-price regime rather than simply a uniform delay. No further postponement was agreed. The European Council conclusions call on the European Commission to update its assessment of ETS2, particularly its design and safeguards. Leaders also demanded action to reduce volatility in the existing carbon market and limit the effect of carbon prices on electricity costs. The outcome stops short of the further postponement sought by several governments, but demonstrates how far energy affordability has moved towards the centre of European climate negotiations. The growing rebellion over ETS2 ETS2 is designed to extend the principle of carbon pricing to fuels used for heating buildings, road transport and certain smaller industrial activities. Unlike the existing Emissions Trading System, which covers large industrial installations and power generation, the new mechanism reaches sectors closely connected to everyday household expenditure. Under the scheme, fuel suppliers must purchase allowances corresponding to the emissions associated with the fuels they sell. Households and motorists will not buy allowances themselves, but suppliers may pass those additional costs through to customers. That distinction is fundamental. A policy designed to encourage investment in cleaner heating systems and vehicles may initially appear to consumers as an increase in petrol, diesel and domestic heating bills. The current legislative timetable provides for ETS2 to become operational in 2028, following an earlier one-year postponement. The latest demands from several Central European governments would push that date back to 2030. Their argument is that consumers and smaller businesses cannot reasonably be expected to absorb another source of energy-price pressure while European economies continue to contend with geopolitical uncertainty, expensive fuel and comparatively weak industrial competitiveness. Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš has been particularly outspoken in his criticism, arguing that carbon pricing risks weakening Europe’s industrial base and making everyday life more expensive. Italy has supported calls for greater flexibility, with Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni presenting the discussion as part of a wider attempt to restore competitiveness and make the transition more affordable. Why other governments opposed another delay The initiative encountered resistance from governments concerned that repeatedly postponing established climate legislation would weaken investment certainty and reduce confidence in European policy. The Nordic member states have been particularly reluctant to reopen the timetable. Their position reflects a broader concern that businesses investing in clean technologies need credible long-term rules, rather than legislation liable to be revised whenever political opposition intensifies. Carbon pricing is intended to change economic incentives gradually. Higher costs for carbon-intensive fuels are supposed to make alternatives such as better-insulated buildings, electric vehicles and cleaner heating more financially attractive. Critics of further postponement argue that delaying implementation would also delay those incentives, potentially increasing the eventual cost of reaching the Union’s emissions-reduction targets. Yet the opposition has exposed a weakness in that argument: consumers cannot always respond quickly to price signals. A household relying on an older heating system or a worker with no practical alternative to driving may face higher costs long before affordable low-carbon options become available. That issue has been central to earlier discussions over ETS2. EU Today reported on stronger carbon-price safeguards in June, when European institutions moved to provide additional market intervention if allowance prices rose sharply. Commission ordered to reassess the economic impact Rather than endorsing a new delay, European leaders have asked the Commission to review ETS2’s economic impact and safeguards. The summit also urged faster progress on adjustments to the Market Stability Reserve, the mechanism intended to help manage the supply of carbon allowances and prevent excessive price volatility. Under the existing scheme, market interventions can increase or reduce allowance availability in response to defined conditions. For ETS2, safeguards are especially politically sensitive because the cost of carbon allowances may ultimately be reflected in household transport and heating expenditure. The European Commission’s updated auction arrangements already envisage auctions of ETS2 allowances beginning in 2027, ahead of the system’s operational launch in 2028. That timetable gives governments a relatively narrow window to settle the remaining political disputes and put protective measures into effect. A central part of the response is the Social Climate Fund, intended to support vulnerable households, transport users and small businesses through investments in energy efficiency, cleaner heating, improved transport and temporary financial assistance. artigo.texto: A few weeks ago, the famed investor Steve Eisman warned that the companies driving the AI boom were using the same financial shenanigans that once brought down Enron in what is still regarded as one of the greatest financial frauds ever. Eisman has credibility when it comes to anticipating economic disasters. As one of the handful of investors who saw the 2008 financial crisis coming, he made an estimated $1 billion betting that the market would collapse. In Michael Lewis’s book The Big Short, and the subsequent movie, Eisman is one of the heroes. Eisman now has a popular Substack as well as a YouTube channel with some 224,000 subscribers. “What I find disturbing is some of the off-balance-sheet financing [vehicles] I thought had gone the way of the dodo bird after the Enron and post-GFC (Great Financial Crisis) debacles,” he told his viewers last month. “Are we going to do this all over again?” Michael Burry is another hero of The Big Short. An early AI bear, he closed his hedge fund last November because his bearish views were not, as he acknowledged at the time, “in sync with the market.” He has since started a Substack called Cassandra Unchained, which has over 300,000 subscribers. But he has never stopped viewing the financing of the AI build-out as a house of cards. Like Eisman, he has been relentlessly pointing out various AI-related financing techniques that are, unquestionably, reminiscent of Enron and the 2008 financial crisis. “History is repeating,” he posted ominously in mid-August. “Time to read this one again or for the first time,” he added, referring to The Smartest Guys in the Room, the 2003 book about the Enron debacle.

artigo.texto: Nordeste avança como polo de data centers no Brasil O Nordeste brasileiro firma-se como um dos principais destinos para a instalação de data centers no país, impulsionado por uma combinação de incentivos fiscais, demanda crescente por processamento de dados e condições energéticas favoráveis. A região deve liderar o crescimento da economia brasileira na próxima década, com o PIB avançando 3,3% ao ano entre 2028 e 2035, bem acima dos 2,4% projetados para o país, segundo projeção da Tendências Consultoria divulgada em junho. Esse dinamismo econômico reflete-se diretamente na expansão da infraestrutura digital, que atrai investimentos de grande porte para estados como Ceará, Bahia e Pernambuco. O cenário nacional também é promissor: como mostrou a CNN, o Brasil deve dobrar a capacidade de seu mercado de data centers até 2030, com boa parte da nova capacidade já contratada antes mesmo de ficar pronta. Ao todo, dos 660 MW (megawatts) que estão em construção no país, 56% estão pré-locados. Essa demanda aquecida beneficia especialmente o Nordeste, que oferece terrenos amplos, energia renovável e incentivos locais, tornando-se uma alternativa competitiva aos tradicionais polos do Sudeste. Incentivos federais impulsionam novos projetos Um marco regulatório recente deve acelerar ainda mais esse movimento. O Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center), nova lei que prevê um programa de incentivos para o setor no país, foi sancionado em setembro pelo presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) e deve estimular a instalação e ampliação dos centros de dados no país. A medida reduz a carga tributária sobre investimentos em infraestrutura digital, tornando projetos no Nordeste ainda mais atrativos para empresas nacionais e estrangeiras. Além dos benefícios fiscais, a região conta com um ambiente macroeconômico favorável. Entre agosto de 2025 e julho deste ano, a região registrou crescimento de 2,5%, liderando o desempenho entre as regiões ao lado do Sul. O resultado supera a média nacional, de 1,5%, e reforça o dinamismo da economia nordestina, segundo análise do Etene (Escritório Técnico de Estudos Econômicos do Nordeste), do Banco do Nordeste (BNB). Esse ritmo de expansão cria um ciclo virtuoso: mais atividade econômica exige mais capacidade de processamento de dados, o que atrai novos data centers. Nordeste concentrará 30% dos novos investimentos A posição estratégica do Nordeste no setor é corroborada por projeções oficiais. Segundo a EPE (Empresa de Pesquisa Energética), o Nordeste deve seguir no centro do debate energético nacional e deve atrair quase 30% dos novos investimentos em data centers de grande porte. A região dispõe de uma matriz elétrica com forte participação de fontes eólicas e solares, o que reduz custos operacionais e atende às metas de sustentabilidade das grandes empresas de tecnologia. Esse potencial já se materializa em projetos concretos. Na capital cearense, o avanço do setor tem entre seus exemplos o TFOR3, da Tecto Data Centers, plataforma de data centers controlada pelo BTG Pactual e ligada à V.tal, que atualmente é o maior centro de dados em operação da região. O empreendimento simboliza a confiança de investidores institucionais no Nordeste como hub digital. Mega Lobster: referência em capacidade e expansão Conhecido como “Mega Lobster”, o empreendimento fica na Praia do Futuro, em Fortaleza, e foi inaugurado em outubro do ano passado. Ao todo, a capacidade final é de 20 MW (megawatts), com a expansão ocorrendo em etapas, acompanhando a demanda dos clientes. A localização privilegiada, próxima aos cabos submarinos de fibra óptica que conectam o Brasil à Europa e à África, reduz a latência nas comunicações internacionais, um diferencial competitivo relevante. Para empresários e comerciantes do interior paulista, o avanço dos data centers no Nordeste pode parecer distante, mas seus efeitos se propagam por toda a cadeia produtiva nacional. A expansão da infraestrutura digital impulsiona a demanda por serviços de tecnologia, equipamentos, construção civil e mão de obra especializada, gerando oportunidades indiretas para fornecedores de outras regiões. Além disso, a melhoria da conectividade e da capacidade de processamento beneficia negócios de todos os portes, inclusive os localizados em cidades como Araçatuba, Birigui e Penápolis, que dependem cada vez mais de serviços em nuvem e comércio eletrônico. O Nordeste, portanto, consolida-se como um polo estratégico para data centers no Brasil, sustentado por incentivos fiscais, crescimento econômico acima da média e vantagens energéticas. À medida que novos projetos saem do papel, a região deve ampliar sua participação no mercado nacional e atrair ainda mais investimentos, reforçando seu papel no desenvolvimento da economia digital brasileira. Perguntas Frequentes Qual é a projeção de crescimento do PIB do Nordeste entre 2028 e 2035? Segundo a Tendências Consultoria, o PIB do Nordeste deve crescer 3,3% ao ano entre 2028 e 2035, acima da média nacional de 2,4%. Qual a participação do Nordeste nos novos investimentos em data centers de grande porte no Brasil? De acordo com a EPE, o Nordeste deve atrair quase 30% dos novos investimentos em data centers de grande porte no país. Qual é o maior data center em operação no Nordeste e qual sua capacidade? O TFOR3, da Tecto Data Centers, localizado na Praia do Futuro em Fortaleza, é o maior data center em operação na região, com capacidade final de 20 MW.

artigo.texto: Climate-vulnerable countries could gain access to US$20 billion in additional annual financing by 2030 through carbon markets. A new handbook aims to help them attract this climate funding ahead of the United Nations climate summit COP31. Released on October 14, 2026, the Article 6 Senior Officials’ Handbook explains how governments can take part in international carbon markets. The Climate Vulnerable Forum and V20 Finance Ministers (CVF-V20) developed it with the Voluntary Carbon Markets Integrity Initiative (VCMI). The initiative addresses a major funding gap. The 77 countries represented by the CVF-V20 face an estimated US$490 billion annual shortfall in financing for their climate plans. Carbon markets could provide another source of funding. But countries need clear rules, strong public institutions, and reliable safeguards to benefit. The handbook offers practical advice to help governments make informed choices and attract investment. However, the US$20 billion figure is a potential opportunity, not guaranteed funding. New Handbook Puts Carbon Finance on the COP31 Agenda The handbook was released in Bangkok during the 2026 Annual Meetings of the World Bank Group and the International Monetary Fund. Its launch came about a month before COP31, which is scheduled for November 9–20 in Antalya, Türkiye. The timing highlights a key challenge for climate action: countries need money to turn their climate plans into real projects. The United Nations Environment Programme has also stressed the need to improve access to climate finance and help communities facing serious climate risks. Many developing countries struggle to attract investment, even when they have clear climate goals. They may lack the laws, technical skills, or project plans needed to secure funding. Carbon markets could help close part of this gap. Countries can earn money by supporting projects that reduce or remove greenhouse gas emissions. These projects may include forest protection, renewable energy, and methane reduction. However, governments must first decide which projects to support and how to manage carbon credit sales. The new handbook aims to help officials understand these choices before making deals. How Article 6 Can Help Countries Raise Money The handbook focuses on Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, which allows countries to work together to cut greenhouse gas emissions. Article 6.2 allows countries to trade authorized emissions reductions through agreements with other countries. Article 6.4 sets up a United Nations-supervised system for issuing carbon credits under an international framework. These rules can help countries attract foreign investment into climate projects. For example, a government can approve a project that cuts emissions. It can let some verified reductions be sold to a buyer in another country. However, these transfers require careful accounting. Countries must follow approval and reporting rules and must also apply corresponding adjustments where required. These adjustments help prevent the same emissions reduction from being counted toward two countries’ climate targets. Governments must also consider how selling carbon credits affects their own climate commitments, known as nationally determined contributions (NDCs). The handbook explains these choices and covers both Article 6.2 agreements and the Article 6.4 mechanism. Sara Jane Ahmed, Managing Director and Finance Advisor of CVF-V20 Secretariat, remarked: “This new handbook specifically responds to the needs of climate-vulnerable countries for specialised and tailored support and guidance on participating in carbon markets. By empowering climate-vulnerable member countries with informed leadership and institutional decision-making, this handbook can help build the policy environment needed to attract much-needed investments through Article 6 of the Paris Agreement.” Eight Modules Guide Governments Through Carbon Market Rules The handbook contains eight modules for senior government officials involved in carbon markets. It covers several important areas: - Project approval: Deciding which projects and emissions reductions can be approved for international transfer. - Revenue: Assessing how carbon markets could raise money for national climate plans. - Benefit-sharing: Deciding how project income and other benefits should be shared. - Environmental and social safeguards: Protecting communities and ensuring projects deliver real climate benefits. - Private investment: Creating conditions that encourage companies and investors to take part. - Laws and oversight: Setting rules and assigning responsibility for managing carbon markets. The handbook also provides country examples and explains common challenges. Governments can use it as a checklist to identify missing rules, skills, or systems before entering the market. This guidance matters because carbon markets involve more than selling credits. Governments must decide who can approve projects, how money will be managed, and how results will be measured. They also need clear rules to protect communities and ensure that projects deliver the benefits they promise. Why Poor Countries Have Had Limited Access to Carbon Market Investment The handbook addresses a long-standing problem: many climate-vulnerable countries have struggled to attract carbon market investment. Forty-five least developed countries made up just 1.5% of projects registered under the Kyoto Protocol’s Clean Development Mechanism, according to the CVF-V20 and VCMI. artigo.texto: Microsoft has withdrawn from the UK’s largest AI data center project in Loughton, Essex over concerns about electricity supplies. Nscale, a British vertically integrated, full-stack AI infrastructure and neocloud company remains committed to the facility’s development which was announced in 2025, and originally expected to be completed in 2027. The project was backed by the UK government as a major part of its plans to expand the UK’s artificial intelligence infrastructure. Microsoft had been expected to fund a supercomputer at the site and act as its anchor customer. Its withdrawal leaves Nscale without an official public customer for the Essex facility. The setback follows reports that electricity supply problems would delay the project’s connection to the national grid as reported by the BBC. “We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK,” Nscale told the BBC. “Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term. This unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts.” Microsoft declined to comment on the partnership termination. Nscale is also reportedly preparing for a potential New York stock market listing this year, with a possible valuation of £ 26 billion (US$ 35 billion). Delays to major projects and the loss of a significant customer could complicate those plans. Microsoft’s withdrawal could create further uncertainty around Nscale’s expansion plans and attract greater investor scrutiny ahead of its planned US initial public offer (IPO) on the New York stock market listing according to the Guardian. The two companies continue to work together on projects in Norway, Portugal and the United States. The withdrawal raises questions about the project’s delivery and Nscale’s wider expansion plans, supported by Nvidia, is among the businesses selected to support the government’s ambition to establish domestic AI computing capacity.

artigo.texto: Batam and Bintan’s widespread outage last Monday was not due to the operational testing of a data center, according to President Director of PT PLN Batam Kwin Fo as quoted by a local daily. “The widespread blackout that occurred on Monday (12/10) on Batam and Bintan islands had nothing to do with a data center. The information that there is testing or commissioning for data center operations, and it requires a lot of power, is not true at all,” Kwin reportedly told reporters in Batam yesterday, after news that the outage was linked to a data center testing was widely circulated in the community. He added that the data center in question is still under development and is not expected to be fully operational in the near future. And if it does start operating, the operational capacity would not exceed 10 per cent of the total capacity of the data center, Kwin said. The data center was not named. PLN Batam is Batam’s electricity utility, a subsidiary of Indonesia’s state-owned electricity company, PT PLN (Persero). Its full name is PT Pelayanan Listrik Nasional Batam; and it supplies electricity in Batam and surrounding areas. Kwin Fo emphasized that Batam’s long-term electricity supply for data centers has been catered for in PLN Batam’s planning. “We do not have a deficit or a shortage of supply. Our power reserves are still around almost 20 percent. Batam’s electricity load is targeted to increase from around 930 MW to more than 1,000 MW. Therefore, we estimate that by the end of 2027, the supply capacity will reach 1,200 to 1,300 MW,” he said. Currently, Batam’s electricity system has a supply capacity of 930MW, with a load of around 780 MW. Thus, the power reserve is still around 20 percent. The growth of electricity demand in Batam has exceeded 15 per cent, much higher than the 3-4 per cent growth of national electricity consumption. “We estimate that in the 2027-2032 range, the load will increase by around 300-400 MW. There is a growth of about 30 percent. To meet the demand, PLN Batam is taking steps to add additional power such as building a new Gas Power Plant (PLTG) and a new Solar Power Plant (PLTS),” he said. Additionally, PLN Batam plans to use a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) or a battery-based energy storage system to support Batam-Bintan electricity. It takes only nnoseconds or milliseconds for the battery to release power which is much faster than a conventional plant such as coal-fired steam power plants (PLTU), Kwin Fo added.

artigo.texto: O início dos testes do primeiro sistema de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) integrado a uma usina solar no Brasil, autorizado pela Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel), representa um marco para a evolução do setor elétrico nacional. Instalado na usina solar Sol de Brotas 7, da Statkraft, na Bahia, o projeto combina geração fotovoltaica e armazenamento de energia, abrindo caminho para novos modelos de operação, maior flexibilidade da rede e uma gestão mais eficiente dos ativos renováveis. + NOTÍCIAS NO GRUPO NM DO WHATSAPP Para a Voltxs Energia, o avanço demonstra que o armazenamento deixa de ser apenas uma tecnologia promissora e passa a integrar as estratégias de desenvolvimento dos empreendimentos renováveis. À medida que a participação das fontes solar e eólica cresce na matriz elétrica brasileira, aumenta também a necessidade de soluções capazes de conferir maior previsibilidade, flexibilidade e eficiência à operação desses ativos. “O início desse projeto representa um passo importante para a maturidade do mercado brasileiro de armazenamento de energia. O BESS deixa de ser apenas um tema de planejamento e passa a ser validado na prática como um componente estratégico para a operação dos ativos renováveis. A combinação entre geração fotovoltaica e armazenamento amplia as possibilidades de gestão da energia produzida e prepara o setor para uma matriz cada vez mais dinâmica”, afirma Matheus Ivanoski Teixeira, Diretor de Operações (COO) da Voltxs Energia. Armazenamento passa a integrar a estratégia dos ativos (bateria) Os sistemas BESS permitem armazenar a energia gerada em momentos de maior produção e disponibilizá-la quando houver necessidade operacional ou maior demanda do sistema elétrico. Na avaliação da Voltxs, o principal ganho está na integração entre geração, armazenamento e gestão inteligente dos ativos. “Quando analisamos um projeto híbrido, não estamos falando apenas da instalação de baterias. O grande diferencial está na capacidade de integrar geração, armazenamento e inteligência operacional para extrair mais eficiência dos ativos. Essa visão tende a se tornar cada vez mais relevante para investidores, operadores e proprietários de usinas”, explica Teixeira. Segundo o executivo, os primeiros projetos em operação terão papel fundamental para fornecer dados reais sobre desempenho, dimensionamento, custos, retorno econômico e aplicações do armazenamento em diferentes cenários. Mercado entra em uma nova fase O avanço também reforça uma tendência observada internacionalmente: a evolução das usinas renováveis para plataformas energéticas mais inteligentes, capazes de combinar diferentes tecnologias e responder de forma mais eficiente às necessidades do sistema elétrico. Na avaliação da Voltxs, essa transformação deve impulsionar novos modelos de negócios, ampliar a competitividade dos empreendimentos renováveis e acelerar investimentos em soluções de armazenamento nos próximos anos. “Os projetos pioneiros serão importantes para definir as melhores estratégias de utilização do armazenamento no Brasil. O aprendizado obtido nessa fase permitirá desenvolver modelos mais eficientes tanto do ponto de vista operacional quanto econômico. A tendência é que a gestão integrada dos ativos passe a ser um diferencial competitivo para o setor”, destaca o COO da Voltxs. Além dos benefícios operacionais, a integração entre geração fotovoltaica e armazenamento fortalece a discussão sobre a modernização da infraestrutura elétrica brasileira, criando condições para uma matriz energética mais flexível, resiliente e preparada para a expansão das fontes renováveis. Sobre a Voltxs Energia A Voltxs Energia atua no mercado de energia com soluções voltadas à gestão estratégica de ativos, eficiência energética e inteligência para o setor elétrico. A empresa desenvolve projetos que combinam tecnologia, análise de dados e conhecimento regulatório para apoiar empresas na otimização de custos, aumento da eficiência operacional e maximização do valor de seus ativos energéticos. artigo.texto: Segundo o site Interesting Engineering (EUA), pesquisadores da Universidade de Limerick (Irlanda) e da Universidade de Valência ( Espanha ) criaram materiais de nanofibras de carbono para uso em baterias de íon-sódio, abrindo um novo caminho para a utilização de subprodutos industriais no desenvolvimento de tecnologias de armazenamento de energia ecologicamente corretas. Utilização de subprodutos do papel como materiais para baterias de íon-sódio. Segundo o site Interesting Engineering (EUA), pesquisadores da Universidade de Limerick (Irlanda) e da Universidade de Valência (Espanha) criaram materiais de nanofibras de carbono para uso em baterias de íon-sódio, abrindo um novo caminho para a utilização de subprodutos industriais no desenvolvimento de tecnologias de armazenamento de energia ecologicamente corretas. A equipe de pesquisa utilizou água como solvente, misturando lignossulfonato — um subproduto da indústria de papel — com gelatina e alginato para criar materiais de eletrodo. Após tratamento térmico, a gelatina e o alginato formaram uma estrutura de carbono porosa com uma grande área superficial, permitindo que os íons de sódio se movessem e fossem armazenados com facilidade. Essa abordagem pode reduzir o impacto ambiental ao substituir solventes orgânicos por água, além de abrir caminho para a utilização de subprodutos da indústria de papel como materiais para baterias de armazenamento de energia. Graças ao seu abundante teor de sódio, espera-se que as baterias de íon-sódio se tornem uma alternativa viável às baterias de íon-lítio, especialmente para sistemas de armazenamento de energia em larga escala. No entanto, o novo material requer uma avaliação mais aprofundada de seu desempenho e aplicações práticas antes da comercialização.

artigo.texto: - The all-new Han measures more than 5.1 meters long, an increase of 161 mm over the Han EV Flash Charging Edition launched in April. - The third-generation Qin Plus EV appears in the filing with a 2,800 mm wheelbase, as BYD begins teasing the new generation. BYD's (HKEX: 1211) all-new Han and third-generation Qin Plus have appeared in Chinese regulatory filings, advancing a refresh of its core sedan lineup. The 2 models were included in the 412th batch of new vehicle filings released by China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology on Friday, revealing their dimensions and powertrain specifications. The all-new Han filings cover 3 battery-electric variants and 1 plug-in hybrid variant, all with 5 seats. The sedan measures 5,156 mm long and 1,969 mm wide, with a wheelbase of 3,030 mm. Compared with the Han EV Flash Charging Edition launched in April, the all-new Han is 161 mm longer and 59 mm wider, with a wheelbase extended by 110 mm. The electric variants offer single-motor rear-wheel drive and dual-motor all-wheel drive. The 2 rear-wheel-drive variants have peak motor outputs of 245 kW and 300 kW, respectively, both with a top speed of 240 km/h. The all-wheel-drive variant pairs a 200 kW front motor with a 320 kW (429 hp) rear motor, for a combined peak output of 520 kW and a top speed of 270 km/h. The plug-in hybrid variant combines a 1.5-liter engine with an electric motor delivering peak power of 200 kW, with a top speed of 200 km/h. The all-new Han in these filings is a separate model from the Da Han launched by BYD on October 13. The Da Han sits higher in the lineup, measuring 5,256 mm long with a 3,130 mm wheelbase. The Han refresh comes amid a sharp decline in the series' sales. September sales totaled 2,529 units, down 70.90% year-on-year and 30.83% from August, according to data compiled by CnEVPost. From January through September, Han series sales totaled 44,324 units, down 68.86% year-on-year, underscoring pressure on BYD to revive the lineup through product updates. Meanwhile, the third-generation Qin Plus variant in the filing is battery-electric. It measures 4,840 mm long, 1,900 mm wide and 1,498 mm tall, with a wheelbase of 2,800 mm. The 5-seat sedan features a permanent-magnet synchronous motor with peak output of 100 kW and a lithium iron phosphate battery, with a top speed of 170 km/h. Lu Tian, general manager of sales for BYD's Dynasty lineup, teased the third-generation Qin Plus on Weibo on Friday, highlighting its larger dimensions and increased space and saying more information would be released in due course. Images accompanying Lu's post showed the third-generation Qin Plus DM-i plug-in hybrid, while the filing documents provided cover the battery-electric Qin Plus EV. The Qin series has already received several updates this year. In January, BYD launched the 2026 Qin Plus DM-i and added longer-range variants to the Qin L DM-i, increasing the maximum CLTC electric range of both hybrid models to 210 km. In August, BYD launched the Qin Max, positioned above the Qin L and available in battery-electric and plug-in hybrid versions, further expanding this core sedan family.

artigo.texto: Energy storage driving global green transition Country builds complete industrial chain amid battery industry expansion By ZHANG YI and HU MEIDONG in Ningde, Fujian | China Daily | Updated: 2026-10-17 07:08 China's booming energy storage sector, propelled by a more than twofold increase in storage battery output in the first half of the year, is helping drive the global green transition and improve the reliability of renewable energy on power grids worldwide, officials and experts said. They made the remarks at the 2026 World Energy Storage Conference, a three-day event that concluded on Friday in Ningde, Fujian province, a major global hub for the advanced energy storage industry. At the conference, Xiong Jijun, vice-minister of industry and information technology, said China's storage battery output rose 110 percent year-on-year to more than 420 gigawatt-hours in the first half of this year. By the end of June, the country's installed capacity of new type energy storage had exceeded 153 million kilowatts, about 50 times the level at the start of the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-25). "China has built a complete industrial chain with over 90 percent of key equipment localized," Xiong said, noting that a diverse technological landscape has emerged, led by lithium batteries alongside sodium-ion and flow battery technologies. He said China would step up efforts to develop new type energy storage during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-30) and welcomed global partners to work together on aligning technologies and standards to advance the global green and low-carbon energy transition. Ilina Stefanova, director of the Coalition for Action at the International Renewable Energy Agency, said China plays a central role in the global energy storage market, accounting for 56 percent of the world's new battery storage capacity additions in 2025. "China's remarkable progress in storage deployment is also helping to change the economics of renewable electricity," Stefanova said. Recent analysis showed that combining solar and wind power with battery storage can provide competitive renewable electricity around the clock, she said. In Hebei province, the cost was estimated at $54 per megawatt-hour in 2025 and could fall to $37 per MWh by 2030. Zou Ciyong, deputy to the director general of the United Nations Industrial Development Organization, echoed that view, saying it is important to ensure that the growth of battery storage translates into better energy services, stronger industrial capabilities and lasting improvements in people's lives. China's experience in areas such as electric vehicle batteries and energy storage offers a valuable basis for international exchange, he said. With its expertise in innovation and manufacturing, Ningde is becoming an important global hub for new energy industries, particularly batteries and energy storage. Ningde is now home to more than 90 enterprises across the lithium battery supply chain. The output value of its lithium battery industry rose from 73.4 billion yuan ($10.98 billion) in 2020 to 303.3 billion yuan last year, according to data presented at the conference. Zeng Yuqun, founder and chairman of CATL, a leading Chinese battery manufacturer based in Ningde, said, "The global energy storage market is experiencing explosive growth." As renewable energy becomes a major source of power worldwide, storage is evolving from a supporting facility into essential infrastructure for power systems, Zeng said. Citing industry data, he said global shipments of energy storage batteries rose 71 percent year-on-year in the first half of this year. For the first time, markets outside China accounted for more than half of the global total, with large-scale deployments expanding rapidly across Europe, the United States and emerging markets. CATL has deployed more than 3,000 energy storage projects worldwide, using more than 500 billion pieces of research and development and testing data to significantly improve grid adaptability and operational reliability, Zeng said.

artigo.texto: In June, as public opinion on data centers soured, Gov. Greg Abbott took his first big swing at reining in the industry, issuing a round of regulatory recommendations to the Legislature that included his call to end a major tax break for the facilities. Donors with ties to the data center industry responded with cash. That same month, they gave Abbott’s campaign $1.5 million. Two months later, the third-term Republican governor toughened his stance by pausing approvals for data centers seeking to connect to the state’s electrical grid, pending a statewide audit. That same month, he said in an interview with ABC that data centers “dug their own grave” and “got the backlash they deserve” for not gaining community buy-in at the outset of projects. More money poured in. After announcing the pause, Abbott went on to receive another $2.8 million from data center-related donors, his biggest monthly haul from the industry over the course of this election cycle, an analysis by The Texas Tribune found. In total, Abbott has raised about $9 million from data center-related donors since July 2025, which accounts for about 13% of the donations he’s taken in during that time. The Tribune vetted the affiliations of every donor who contributed at least $25,000 to Abbott or his Democratic opponent Gina Hinojosa since July 2025. More than half of Abbott’s data center haul, or $4.9 million, came from people or companies (and their corporate political action committees) that develop, own or operate data centers. That group includes people like Rhett Bennett, the CEO of Black Mountain, a Fort Worth-based energy company building hyperscale data centers across Texas. Bennett and Black Mountain gave a combined $1 million to Abbott since last July. The group also includes people like Toby Neugebauer — the former CEO of Fermi America, the company behind the massive Project Matador data center campus in the Panhandle — who contributed $100,000 to Abbott. The other $4.1 million in donations came from donors the Tribune found to have indirect data center links: people and companies that invest in or have financial ties to data centers, are associated with companies that primarily develop AI, or whose business models involve, at least in part, serving or helping build data centers. That group includes people like Jeff Yass, a GOP megadonor best known for his interest in expanding school vouchers, but whose investment portfolio contains a number of companies that rely heavily on AI or data center technology. Yass’ investment firm Susquehanna International Group has stakes in Bytedance, the parent company of TikTok that also develops its own AI models; Broadcom, a company that supplies hardware and infrastructure to data centers; and Alphabet, Inc, the parent company of Google, which owns and operates data centers. This group also includes Edward Roski Jr., president of Majestic Realty Corp, a commercial real estate development company that counts data centers among its diverse list of tenants. They both gave Abbott $1 million. Identifying data center donors is imperfect because many people with ties to the industry also have other business interests or political motivations. For example, Abbott’s largest data center-related donor was Airbnb co-founder Joe Gebbia, who contributed $1.5 million. Gebbia is a board member of Tesla, which owns and operates its own data centers. Abbott has also received major data center-linked donations from megadonors Elon Musk and Harlan Crow, who are both active in advancing conservative politics. Musk, the CEO of Tesla, which operates AI data centers, gave Abbott $500,000 and Crow, who has been an Abbott donor long before the recent data center buildout, gave $250,000. Crow is the chair of the board and former CEO of Crow Family Holdings, which announced in January it was developing a data center campus in central Dallas with CleanArc Data Centers. “Mr. Crow has been a steadfast and long-standing supporter of Gov. Greg Abbott, dating back well over a decade and across several campaigns,” Crow’s office said to the Tribune. The affiliations have nonetheless proven to be a liability for Abbott this election year. As the explosion in data center development in Texas fuels bipartisan discontent, candidates up and down the ballot, on both sides of the aisle, have worked to distance themselves from the industry while weaponizing donations from data centers against their opponents. Staring down polling that has him neck-in-neck with Hinojosa, Abbott is for the first time fighting for his political life, trying to strike a balance between cracking down on the facilities while still holding onto his pro-business ethos. “Governor Abbott has made his position on data centers clear. Data centers must pay their own way, protect Texas’ electric grid, bring their own water, and not to disturb the communities where they operate,” said Abbott campaign spokesman Eduardo Leal to the Tribune. “The Governor also directed state agencies to issue no data center related permits until ERCOT completes its review and he has also called for ending outdated taxpayer-funded incentives. Those are the standards Governor Abbott has laid out, and those remain his priorities.” Leal also called the Tribune’s reporting a “disingenuous attempt to manufacture controversy out of information that is not new.” Hinojosa, meanwhile, has made connecting Abbott to data centers a central part of her attack. “Greg Abbott invited data centers into Texas with the richest tax breaks in the country, took millions of dollars in donations from the data center interests, and has spent months lying to Texans about his record to save his political career,” Hinojosa said. “Texans know I’ll fight for them – not the big corporations – and ensure they have a seat at the table to decide if and how data centers come into their communities.” In a campaign ad, Hinojosa accuses Abbott of taking $20 million from “data center executives and companies.” Th

artigo.texto: Is Finland’s data center boom getting out of hand? In early September, Google announced that it would invest €13 billion in Finland and build data centers in several locations. It would be the largest investment in Finnish economic history. This was big news and politicians were grateful. The Finnish economy has been depressed for years and investments are needed. By October, the atmosphere had changed and Google’s construction site stood still. It had turned out that a forest on the site had been cut down and work had started — despite the fact that Google hadn’t yet secured permission or submitted the environmental impact assessment required by law. The company had been in a huge hurry, which appears to have backfired. In Finland, the debate surrounding the construction of data centers is getting increasingly heated. It is almost impossible to keep up with how quickly data center plans are appearing all over the country. Since Google, there have been other announcements of the same magnitude involving billions upon billions of euros. In mid-October, the number of data center plans was somewhere between 150 and 200. Different sources use different figures, and there is no exact up-to-date information available. Most of them were still just plans, but construction is going on in many locations. The news headlines are listing American giants like Google, Meta and Microsoft, but there are also Finnish or international companies that have emerged, suddenly announcing their intention to invest billions in remote corners of small municipalities. Decision-making on data centers is highly decentralised in Finland. Companies approach small municipalities one by one. These are often places where decision-makers are used to people and jobs gradually disappearing into large cities. Then, suddenly, someone appears at their door promising a huge investment in the municipality and a lot of new jobs. At that point, it is very difficult to say no. Finland’s new reality As a result, the whole thing has gotten out of hand. Finland is gradually waking up to a new reality in which excavators are roaring along the country’s outlying regions, and in some cities building data centers — the owners and users of which are typically somewhere far away. What are the benefits that remain in Finland, and what are the risks? Among decision-makers and the general public, the reactions have ranged from enthusiasm to horror, not to mention confusion. The Finnish economy has been depressed for a long time, and new investments have been desperately needed. But the data center boom is so big that it’s already raising suspicions. Where does all the electricity come from? Where would all the builders come from? Will Finland be made into a sort of colony of data centers, which after completion employ only a few people and consume a large part of Finland’s electricity production and whose benefits drain abroad? Companies are drawn to Finland by the northern climate, which helps to cool the data centers. Companies are also attracted by the fact that electricity is readily available, and its production is often emission-free thanks to nuclear power, hydropower or wind power. Finns, on the other hand, are beginning to worry about whether there really is electricity available for all this, while people also want to have low electricity prices. Many of the new data center plans are in northern Finland. For example, Google’s new locations are Kajaani, Vaala and Muhos. Of these, Kajaani is a small town with an industrial tradition. Vaala is deep in the country, and Muhos is located quite close to Oulu — the largest city in the region. Key locations All of these places have one thing in common: they are close to good electricity transmission networks. In each case, there are municipalities nearby where other companies are planning data centers of the same size. Locations in Northern Finland (but mainly outside Lapland, the northernmost region of the country) have to do with the structure of the electricity transmission network. There are large trunk lines in that area that can be joined. Especially in Northern Finland, it has been noticed that “green transition” often refers to the appearance of windmills on the landscape or some other activity where one’s own area is seen only as a source of resources or raw materials. In Eastern Finland, on the other hand, there is concern that due to the structure of the electricity transmission network, new investments won’t be made in the area whose economy suffers the most from the break-up of connections with Russia anyway. Looking at the bigger picture, this debate is also related to the strategic independence of Europe. The companies and users behind the data centers are primarily in America. How does this fit into Europe’s desire to reduce its technological dependence on the U.S.? In October, Finland hurriedly began to prepare a new law which would significantly slow down the connection of data centers to the electricity network and thereby slow down their construction. As a result, the Finnish data center boom appears to have reached a temporary limit, though no one knows the outcome of all this yet. Any opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of Arctic Today. Markku Heikkilä is the Head of Science Communications at the Arctic Centre, University of Lapland, in Rovaniemi. As a former journalist at the Kaleva newspaper in Oulu, Heikkilä has followed Arctic cooperation from its early stages, and he received the State Award for Public Information for his work. He has written several books on these topics. The latest, Once We Had the Arctic – Journeys and Stories from the North, is available in English as an audiobook and e-book.
